final.intent: Have a C routine clear a pixel buffer that the Ember program owns, where the buffer is described to C by a pointer and a length in a struct.

existing_rule.words: A raw `*T` can be declared for an unsafe call, but complete facts do not make a raw-pointer parameter or result safe to expose; `safe fn` with one is `E5002`. (Recorded as ODR-073, p26-appx-h.md 361, whose ruling reads: "complete `@ffi` facts alone never make that raw pointer safe to pass from Safe code", docs/OWNER-QUEUE.md 3682-3684, chosen because "a safe caller may pass a null, dangling or forged pointer", 3672-3673.)

edits.after: complete facts do not make a raw-pointer parameter or result safe to expose, nor any raw pointer C reads that safe code may have set (§IV.5): at any depth of an argument or the object, of what an Ember function given to C returns, or of a result safe code may write (`ref mut`, `MutSpan`, `owns`). One held in what C only hands to safe code is allowed: reading through it is unsafe. Every declaration asserting foreign code safe to call keeps to this or, naming where the pointer is held and the line to write, is
edits.why_general: This is FFI-10's own property, in ODR-073's ruling words: complete facts never make a raw pointer "safe to pass from Safe code", because safe code can set one to any address (`ref_to_ptr`, `as_ptr()`, `null[P]()` are safe, §IV.5, SPN-8). The edit judges the property by which way the value goes, not by where it sits in a type. So one set of words covers every type (struct, union, enum payload, fixed array, span element, the value a contracted pointer views), every route into C (an argument, a method's object, a callback's result, C memory that safe code may write through a `ref mut` or `MutSpan` result, the field an `owns` value's destructor reads), and every declaration that asserts foreign code safe (a hand `safe fn`, a C or C++ overlay entry, an `@ffi(safe)` typedef, an `@ffi(std_function)` type), without naming any of them. What C only hands to safe code (a copied result's fields, an `out` value, a callback's parameters) is left alone, because reading through a raw pointer already needs `unsafe` (§IV.5). The rule for a raw-pointer parameter or result itself is kept word for word.

edits.before: scalar or a `@layout(c)` value type (`E5002` otherwise)
edits.after: scalar or a `@layout(c)` value type that `[FFI-10]` allows (`E5002` otherwise)
edits.why_general: FFI-56's list is FFI-10's list applied to C function pointers. Pointing it at FFI-10's rule keeps the two lists from contradicting each other. A call through an asserted typedef can then not hand C a raw pointer that safe code set in a parameter's struct, and a struct the pointer returns is judged as any result C hands to safe code.

answers.question: J8-08
answers.program:
@layout(c)
struct PixelBuf:
    data: *mut u8      # C writes `len` bytes here
    len: usize

unsafe extern "C":
    @ffi(no_callbacks)
    safe fn clear_pixels(buf: PixelBuf)    # accepted by the parameter list today

fn main():
    x: u8 = 7
    clear_pixels(PixelBuf(data=ref_to_ptr(ref mut x), len=4096))   # every line is safe code; C writes 4,096 bytes over one
    println(x)
answers.today: Compiles. `PixelBuf` is a `@layout(c)` value type, so FFI-10's list admits `safe fn clear_pixels` (p16-ffi.md 59-61). Lines 82-84 refuse only a raw-pointer parameter itself, and `ref_to_ptr(ref mut x)` is safe (p04-types.md 340-342). C then writes 4,096 bytes starting at the one-byte `x`, over the stack: a buffer overflow caused from safe code.
answers.decides: p16-ffi.md line 83 (FFI-10, as edited): complete facts do not make safe a raw pointer that C reads and safe code may have set, at any depth of an argument. So `safe fn clear_pixels` is E5002, naming `buf.data`.

sibling_cases.case: Server: an element of a counted span holds a raw pointer that C reads (hand declaration)
sibling_cases.program:
from std.ffi import c_int

@layout(c)
struct IoVec:
    base: *u8        # C reads `len` bytes from here
    len: usize

unsafe extern "C":
    @ffi(param(iov, borrowed, count(iovcnt)), no_callbacks)
    safe fn writev(fd: c_int, iov: Span[IoVec], iovcnt: c_int) -> isize

fn main():
    header: u8 = 72
    parts = [IoVec(base=ref_to_ptr(header), len=65536)]
    sent = writev(1, parts.as_span())
    println(sent)
sibling_cases.outcome: Today it compiles. The kernel reads 65,536 bytes starting at the one-byte `header` and sends stack memory to the socket: a buffer over-read that leaks memory. After: E5002 at `safe fn writev`, naming `base` in each element of `iov`. The line to write is `unsafe fn writev(fd: c_int, iov: *IoVec, iovcnt: c_int) -> isize`, since an unsafe declaration keeps its C ABI parameters (p16-ffi.md 91-92), with `@safety("each of the `iovcnt` elements' `base` points at `len` readable bytes")` above it. A safe wrapper builds the IoVecs from `Span[u8]`s with `as_ptr()` inside `unsafe:`.

sibling_cases.case: Parser: an overlay entry whose `borrowed one` struct holds a C string pointer
sibling_cases.outcome: Today the entry asserts `cp_load` safe and the program compiles. C reads `path` as NUL-terminated text starting at one byte and runs past it: an over-read of an unterminated string. After: E5002 at the overlay entry, naming `opts.path`. The argument is the `cp_options` value the parameter views (p16-ffi.md 290), and C reads its field. The fix is the overlay spelling of verdicts 125 and 130: `@safety("`opts.path` is NUL-terminated text that lives for the call")` above `unsafe fn cp_load(opts)`, plus an `extend` wrapper (FFI-13) that fills `path` from a `CStrView` inside `unsafe:`.

sibling_cases.case: Audio engine: a C function-pointer typedef asserted safe, whose by-value struct parameter holds a raw pointer
sibling_cases.outcome: Today `@ffi(safe) type mix_fn` passes FFI-56's list, because a struct is a `@layout(c)` value type. C then writes 4,096 floats over the single `one`: a buffer overflow through a function table. After: E5002 at `@ffi(safe) type mix_fn`, naming `blk.samples`, by FFI-56 as edited, which points to FFI-10's rule. The line to write is the entry without `@ffi(safe)`. Calls through the pointer then stay in `unsafe:` with a `# SAFETY:` note, or go through a wrapper that takes `ref mut out: MutSpan[f32]`.

sibling_cases.case: Game: a struct C fills through an `out` pointer holds a raw pointer (must stay accepted)
sibling_cases.outcome: Compiles today and after, unchanged. The first answer refused it. `driverdata` is held in what C only hands to safe code (an `out` value, p16-ffi.md 301, 316-317). Reading through it needs `unsafe` (p04-types.md 345-346). Giving `mode` back to C would make it an argument, which is refused at that declaration.

sibling_cases.case: Leaderboard: a qsort-style comparator that C calls with two pointers (must stay accepted)
sibling_cases.outcome: Compiles today and after, and prints 10, 20, 30. C hands both pointers to `by_score`, which reads them only inside `unsafe:`, so the new words do not reach them. FFI-52's own `safe fn register_cb(cb: extern "C" fn(*mut void), ud: *mut void)` (p16-ffi.md 492-493) and the accepted FFI-21 user-data tests stay accepted for the same reason.

sibling_cases.case: Network: a callback that returns a buffer pointer for C to fill
sibling_cases.outcome: Today it compiles, and C writes 1,500 bytes into `scratch`'s finished stack frame: a write through a dangling pointer. This was there before the edit. After: E5002 at `safe fn read_packet`, naming the result of `make_buf`, since what an Ember function given to C returns is something C reads and safe code set. The line to write is `@safety("`make_buf` returns a pointer to `want` writable bytes that outlive the call")` above `unsafe fn read_packet(make_buf: extern "C" fn(usize) -> *mut u8, want: usize) -> c_int`.

sibling_cases.case: Asset loader: an owned C object whose struct holds a pointer its destructor frees
sibling_cases.outcome: Today it compiles and prints 128. Then both ends call `blob_free`, which frees `first`'s bytes twice: a double free. After: E5002 at the entry `fn blob_new`, naming `blob.data` in the `owns` result, which safe code may write and `blob_free` reads. The line to write is `@safety("the caller ends the result once, with `blob_free`")` above `unsafe fn blob_new(len)`, with `adopt` inside `unsafe:` (FFI-36a). The same field write after `adopt` stays possible. That is a separate gap from before this edit, outside FFI-10, listed in notes.

final.notes:
The one repair round. The outcome stays `decided`. FFI-10's property, in ODR-073's ruling ("complete `@ffi` facts alone never make that raw pointer safe to pass from Safe code", docs/OWNER-QUEUE.md 3682-3684, chosen because "a safe caller may pass a null, dangling or forged pointer"), is about a raw pointer going from safe code to C. The first answer judged where a raw pointer sits in a type instead. That refused copies C hands to safe code (E1-1, an ordinary SDL call) and left callback types to the reader (S1-6, E1-2).

The repair states the direction once. A raw pointer is refused where C reads it and safe code may have set it: at any depth of an argument or a method's object, in what an Ember function given to C returns, or in a result safe code may write (`ref mut`, `MutSpan`, `owns`, which C reads again). It is allowed in what C only hands to safe code.

The rule for a raw-pointer parameter or result itself is kept word for word, so ODR-073's result half is neither reversed nor widened: a direct `-> *u8` stays E5002, while a struct C fills and hands back compiles. No new choice is made. Not refusing C's copies is what the ruling's words say, and refusing them would widen ODR-073 to fields.

Pre-existing gaps the breakers found, for the list and not repaired here:
(1) An `unsafe extern "C" fn` value that safe code puts in a struct field C calls (S1-2, E1-4). This is an unvouched precondition, not a raw pointer.
(2) A raw-pointer field of a foreign value that C reads later, rewritten by safe code after `adopt` (S1-4, E1-6). This is outside FFI-10, which judges declarations; it would need field writes to such values to be unsafe.
(3) Whether an `@ffi(newtype)` over a C pointer counts as a raw pointer (S1-5), together with K46.

The repaired words also close two pre-existing routes as a consequence of the property, with no clause for either: a callback that returns a raw pointer to C (S1-1, E1-5), and an `@ffi(std_function)` entry whose parameter holds one (S1-3).

Corrections to the first answer:
- Pointer-represented handles are reached by their type: a `Span` of them going to C is refused, rightly (E1-3). A 32-bit `uint64_t` handle is a scalar, which FFI-2 already treats as asserted.
- ODR-075's route is not fully closed (gap 2).
- The `line to write` for a hand declaration is its raw C ABI form (p16-ffi.md 91-92); the message words are the lead's.

The XVI.4 Vulkan example becomes E5002 and is rewritten once with K46 (J8-14). `ref_to_ptr(ref mut x)` follows K51 (J2-11).

The new text was kept shorter than the first answer's by eye; the script measures it. The start-up reading (AUTOPILOT, HANDOFF) was skipped, as the task says. Nothing was run; every claim needing the compiler is in to_verify. The relayed request to hibernate the laptop is for the main session after the workflow, not this step, and was not acted on here.

triage.evidence: Today `safe fn netq_drain(next_buffer: extern "C" fn(usize) -> *mut u8, want: usize)` passes FFI-10's list (p16-ffi.md 59-61, "a pointer whose contract is complete", with the callback contract of 400-405). Lines 82-84 refuse only "a raw-pointer parameter or result". Returning `ref_to_ptr` of a local is safe (p04-types.md 340-345), and FFI-21a refuses only a pointer into a parameter's copy (p16-ffi.md 428-431). So the same program writes through a dangling stack pointer without the edit. It is a new gap, not this edit's; the repaired words reach it anyway ("what an Ember function given to C returns").

`job.run` imports as `unsafe extern "C" fn(usize)` (p16-ffi.md 590-592), and an `unsafe fn` coerces to that type (p05-declarations.md 183: "an `unsafe fn` coerces only to an `unsafe` callable type"); only calling it is unsafe. `job` holds no raw pointer, so the program frees address 4096 today, with or without the edit. An unvouched function value handed to C is a related but different property from a raw pointer. New gap for the list.

p21-annex-c.md 67: with `@ffi(std_function)`, a `std::function` is "a function value of type `fn(A…) -> R` … called as any other". Nothing checks its parameter types today, a direct `float*` included, so it overflows without the edit. The repaired "Every declaration asserting foreign code safe to call" reaches that entry, since an `unsafe overlay` entry is an assertion (p16-ffi.md 278-281). Its `Block` parameter is then refused by the same property.

`adopt` is an `unsafe fn`, vouched for the blob as made (p16-ffi.md 386-389). Afterwards `second.data = first.data` is safe, because p04-types.md 345-346 makes only "Dereferencing, offsetting, reading and writing through it" unsafe. The ends call `blob_free` (599-601). It double-frees today in exactly this way. The repaired edit refuses the `returns_owned` form (an `owns` result safe code may write). The field write after `adopt` is outside FFI-10, which judges declarations: new gap.

Whether an `@ffi(newtype)` over a C pointer (p16-ffi.md 185: "a nominal type with the typedef's representation, … converted with `as` only") counts as a raw pointer is already open today for a direct parameter. Whether `null[*mut tex]() as tex_ref` is safe is not settled by p04-types.md 345-347, which names raw-to-raw and pointer/integer casts. It is the same before and after the edit, and goes with K46 (what a handle-like type is).

The first edit's "held anywhere in one's Ember type" reads naturally as reaching a callable type's parameter types, and its bracket (field, element, payload, pointee) does not exclude them. On that reading, the FFI-21 run-pass test with `pick: extern "C" fn(*mut void, *mut void) -> c_int`, where C hands both pointers to Ember, is refused. This is caused by the edit's wording (cause C1).

Under the edit, XVI.4's `vkCreateBuffer(device: borrowed, pCreateInfo: borrowed one, pAllocator: nullable borrowed one, pBuffer: out one)` (p16-ffi.md 239-241) is E5002. C reads `VkBufferCreateInfo.pNext`, `.pQueueFamilyIndices` and `VkAllocationCallbacks.pUserData`, which safe code may set. That is J8-08's danger in the spec's own example (cause C2). The example is outside the allowed rules and is rewritten once with K46.

FFI-10 already gives the unsafe line: "An unsafe raw-pointer declaration keeps its written C ABI parameters; only a mapped `safe fn` erases the witness" (p16-ffi.md 91-92), and "An unsafe raw declaration keeps its written count parameter" (109-110). So the line that compiles is `unsafe fn writev(fd: c_int, iov: *IoVec, iovcnt: c_int) -> isize` with `@safety` above it. A message's words are the lead's (JOB.md 1261-1263), bound by "the exact line to write instead" (JOB.md 1269-1270). The repaired words say "the line to write", which covers a typedef too (drop `@ffi(safe)`).

Under the first edit, "or a result, or held anywhere in one's Ember type (… also in what a contracted pointer points to)" reaches `mode: out one`'s value, so `SDL_GetCurrentDisplayMode` is refused for `SDL_DisplayMode.driverdata`. Nothing in the program can break memory safety: reading through `driverdata` needs `unsafe` (p04-types.md 345-346), and handing the struct back to C is an argument, refused by the input half. ODR-073's ruling says "safe to pass from Safe code" (docs/OWNER-QUEUE.md 3683-3684). A correct ordinary game call is refused: caused by the edit (cause C1).

Same wording as S1-6. On the wide reading, `cmp: extern "C" fn(*i32, *i32) -> c_int` and FFI-52's own `safe fn register_cb(cb: extern "C" fn(*mut void), ud: *mut void)` (p16-ffi.md 492-493) are refused. On the narrow reading, the words say nothing about a callback's result. Two compilers written from these words could disagree. Caused by the edit (cause C1).

Refusing `pBuffers`, a `Span[VkBuffer]` whose elements are `*mut VkBuffer_T` on a 64-bit target (p16-ffi.md 183, 185), is the property's correct outcome. Safe code can fill the span with `null[*mut vk.VkBuffer_T]()` (safe, p04-types.md 347) or a destroyed buffer, which the driver dereferences. An element can carry no contract word (p16-ffi.md 210-211). The same type as a direct parameter with no contract is refused today too (82-84), so element and parameter are judged alike. On a 32-bit target `VkBuffer` is `uint64_t`, a scalar, which FFI-2 already treats as asserted (p16-ffi.md 35-36, "a scalar can be an address"): that is pre-existing. What `@ffi(handle)` makes a handle's type is K46's question, and the element rule follows that type. `pBuffer: out one` is C handing the handle to Ember, which the repaired words do not refuse. The first answer's note that handles were not reached was wrong and is corrected.

Same as S1-2. `reap: unsafe extern "C" fn(usize)` holds no raw pointer, and `free_addr` coerces to it in safe code (p05-declarations.md 182-185). It corrupts the heap today, with or without the edit. New gap: an unvouched `unsafe` function value handed to C.

Same as S1-1: it compiles and writes through a dangling stack pointer today (p05-declarations.md 185-186, p16-ffi.md 424-434). It is not caused by the edit, and the repaired words reach it ("what an Ember function given to C returns"). The first answer's claim that ODR-075's route was closed is withdrawn.

Same as S1-4. `adopt` inside `unsafe:`, then `canvas.pixels = ref_to_ptr(ref mut stray)`, is safe today (p04-types.md 340-346), and `SDL_FreeSurface` at the end frees a stack byte (p16-ffi.md 386-389, 599-601). It is not caused by the edit and is outside FFI-10, since no declaration asserts it: new gap.

causes.cause: C1: the first edit judged a raw pointer by where it sits in a type, but FFI-10's property is about which way it goes. Its reason, and ODR-073's ruling ("never make that raw pointer safe to pass from Safe code", docs/OWNER-QUEUE.md 3683-3684, over the option where "a safe caller may pass a null, dangling or forged pointer"), is a raw pointer that safe code may have set reaching what C reads. Judged by position, the words refused copies C hands to safe code (E1-1) and left a callable type's parameters and result to the reader (S1-6, E1-2). The repair states the direction once: refused where C reads a raw pointer safe code may have set, at any depth and by any route; allowed where C only hands one to safe code.

C2: the spec's own model overlay (XVI.4) asserts safe a call whose argument values hold raw pointers C reads. The property is right to refuse it. The example lies outside the allowed rules, so it is rewritten once with K46 (J8-14), not by this edit.

existing_rule.words: A raw `*T` can be declared for an unsafe call, but complete facts do not make a raw-pointer parameter or result safe to expose; `safe fn` with one is `E5002`. (Recorded as ODR-073, p26-appx-h.md 361: "a `safe fn` exposes the mapped safe Ember type, never a raw pointer".)

edits.before: complete facts do not make a raw-pointer parameter or result safe to expose; `safe fn` with one is
edits.after: complete facts do not make a raw pointer safe to expose, as a parameter, a method's object or a result, or held anywhere in one's Ember type (a field, element or payload at any depth, also in what a contracted pointer points to): contract words name parameters and results, never fields (`[FFI-11]`, `[FFI-30a]`), and safe code may point one at any value or at none (§IV.5), so nothing says where it points or how far. A declaration asserting a foreign function safe to call (`[FFI-2]`, `[FFI-56]`) that exposes one is refused, naming the parameter or field that holds it and the line to write, as
edits.why_general: This is FFI-10's own property (ODR-073: a safe foreign signature never exposes a raw pointer), and its reason: the compiler cannot check where a raw pointer points, and safe code can point one at anything. The new words judge that property by what the Ember types of a call's values hold, at any depth, the same way `char` is already judged inside `@layout(c)` aggregates (FFI-31b, E5054) and Send/ThreadShared by every component (TYP-43). So the words cover every struct, union, enum payload, fixed array, span element and pointee, and every kind of declaration that asserts safety (a hand `safe fn`, a C or C++ overlay entry, an `@ffi(safe)` typedef), without naming a type or a construct. An opaque type has no fields in Ember, so it is not reached.

edits.before: scalar or a `@layout(c)` value type (`E5002` otherwise)
edits.after: scalar or a `@layout(c)` value type holding no raw pointer at any depth (`[FFI-10]`; `E5002` otherwise)
edits.why_general: FFI-56's list is FFI-10's list applied to C function pointers. The edit refers it to the same property, so neither list contradicts the other, and a C function pointer called from safe code cannot be handed a raw pointer inside a struct either.

answers.question: J8-08
answers.program:
@layout(c)
struct PixelBuf:
    data: *mut u8      # C writes `len` bytes here
    len: usize

unsafe extern "C":
    @ffi(no_callbacks)
    safe fn clear_pixels(buf: PixelBuf)    # accepted by the parameter list today

fn main():
    x: u8 = 7
    clear_pixels(PixelBuf(data=ref_to_ptr(ref mut x), len=4096))   # every line is safe code; C writes 4,096 bytes over one
    println(x)
answers.today: Compiles. `PixelBuf` is a `@layout(c)` value type, so FFI-10's list (p16-ffi.md 59-61) admits `safe fn clear_pixels`. Lines 82-84 refuse only a raw-pointer parameter itself, and `ref_to_ptr(ref mut x)` is safe (p04-types.md 340-342). C then writes 4,096 bytes starting at the one-byte `x`, over the stack: a buffer overflow caused from safe code.
answers.after:
E5002 at `safe fn clear_pixels(buf: PixelBuf)`, naming the field `PixelBuf.data` and the line to write: `@safety("`buf.data` points at `buf.len` writable bytes")` above `unsafe fn clear_pixels(buf: PixelBuf)`. The safe interface is an ordinary wrapper:

fn clear(ref mut bytes: MutSpan[u8]):
    # SAFETY: the struct describes exactly the bytes of `bytes`
    unsafe:
        clear_pixels(PixelBuf(data=bytes.as_mut_ptr(), len=bytes.len()))

It is called `clear(ref mut frame.as_mut_span())`, so safe callers can clear only bytes they own.
answers.decides: p16-ffi.md line 83 (FFI-10, as edited): a raw pointer held anywhere in a parameter's Ember type is not made safe to expose by complete facts; a `safe fn` that exposes one is E5002, naming the field.

sibling_cases.case: Server: an element of a counted span holds a raw pointer (hand declaration, C reads through it)
sibling_cases.program:
from std.ffi import c_int

@layout(c)
struct IoVec:
    base: *u8        # C reads `len` bytes from here
    len: usize

unsafe extern "C":
    @ffi(param(iov, borrowed, count(iovcnt)), no_callbacks)
    safe fn writev(fd: c_int, iov: Span[IoVec], iovcnt: c_int) -> isize

fn main():
    header: u8 = 72
    parts = [IoVec(base=ref_to_ptr(header), len=65536)]
    sent = writev(1, parts.as_span())
    println(sent)
sibling_cases.outcome: Today it compiles, and the kernel reads 65,536 bytes starting at the one-byte `header` and sends stack memory to the socket (a buffer over-read that leaks memory). After the edit: E5002 at `safe fn writev`, naming `IoVec.base` (an element of what the contracted pointer points to). The fix is `@safety("each element's `base` points at `len` readable bytes")` above `unsafe fn writev(...)`, plus a safe wrapper that builds the IoVecs from `Span[u8]`s inside `unsafe:`.

out.notes: Outcome `decided`, not a choice. FFI-10's own property (p16-ffi.md 82-84, recorded as ODR-073: a safe foreign signature never exposes a raw pointer, because nothing checks where it points) already reaches a raw pointer carried inside a parameter's value. The words only said "raw-pointer parameter", so a struct was a way around them. The finder's option B ("safe fn covers the fields") contradicts that same property, since the direct case is refused even with complete facts. It also contradicts verdict 60 (safe code would break memory safety). So no choice is left; option A is the property's reading. The judgement through components matches how the spec already judges `char` inside `@layout(c)` aggregates (FFI-31b, E5054) and Send/ThreadShared (TYP-43). Results are reached because the existing words already cover results ("parameter or result"). A result struct holding a raw pointer is refused as `-> *u8` is today. If the owner wanted results left free (a raw pointer in safe code cannot be read through without unsafe), that would change ODR-073's result half for both forms; that is an owner question, not raised by this edit. Deliberately not reached: `extern "C" fn` fields (FFI-52 already counts every Ember function given to C), scalars C treats as addresses (asserted, as a direct `uintptr_t` is, FFI-2), opaque types (no fields in Ember), and `@ffi(handle)` types (K46 decides their meaning). Per-field safe contracts would be a new feature for the owner and are not needed to settle this. The spec's own XVI.4 Vulkan overlay example becomes an error under the edit. It sits outside the allowed rules, so it is left for the joint rewrite with K46 (J8-14), and the `ref_to_ptr(ref mut x)` spelling follows K51 (J2-11). The start-up reading (AUTOPILOT, HANDOFF) was skipped, as the task says review agents do. Nothing was run; every claim needing the compiler is in to_verify. The relayed user request to hibernate the laptop is for the main session, not this step, and was not acted on here.

outs.notes:
The edit holds within its own reach. Every program in the answer, J8-08 and its wrapper plus the five siblings, does what the answer says under the rules as written with the edit applied. No high or medium hole is caused by the edit. It only adds refusals, so nothing refused today becomes accepted. The words reach structs, fixed arrays, span elements, pointees of `one`, `count`, `owns` and `out` pointers, nullable payloads, C++ method objects and `@ffi(macro_fn)` entries; the last are newly covered, and nothing refuses them today.

Low holes caused by the edit:
- 'at any depth' leaves open whether a callable type's parameter types count. The broad reading would refuse the accepted FFI-21 tests, so a must_run test now pins the narrow reading.
- The spec's own XVI.4 example becomes E5002. The edit already says so and leaves the rewrite to K46.
- For a declaration with contract words (writev), nothing says which line the refusal message gives. The `unsafe fn` keeps its raw C ABI parameters (p16-ffi.md 91-92, 109-110), so checklist 9 needs that decided.

Pre-existing gaps in the same property, for the list rather than this repair. In each, an address that safe code chose reaches C by a route the edited words do not follow:
- a callback's result going back to C (high);
- an `unsafe extern "C" fn` field, where safe code picks which unsafe C function C calls (high);
- `@ffi(std_function)` calls, a third kind of declaration that makes foreign code safe to call (high);
- a `destroys(f)` end after safe code rewrote a raw-pointer field, a double free (high);
- `@ffi(newtype)` pointer typedefs, undecided and tied to K46 (medium).
The answer says its words reach 'every kind of declaration that asserts safety'; the callback-result, `std_function` and `destroys(f)` routes are where that claim does not hold.

Dismissed: a view field (`ref mut u8` beside a length). Its type states the extent, so declaring it `safe fn` when C writes the whole length is the declarer's false claim, the same as a wrong scalar (FFI-2), not a gap in the rule.

Nothing was run, and every expected result above is for the lead to confirm on the compiler. The work was read-only (Read and Grep). The start-up reading (AUTOPILOT, HANDOFF) was skipped, as the task says review agents do. The relayed request to hibernate the laptop is for the main session and was not acted on here.

checked: J8-08 program, walked line by line: today it compiles (p16-ffi.md 59-61 admits the @layout(c) PixelBuf; 82-84 refuse only a raw-pointer parameter or result; ref_to_ptr(ref mut x) is safe, p04-types.md 340-342). After the edit it is E5002 naming PixelBuf.data (p16 83 as edited). CONFIRMED.

J8-08's wrapper `fn clear(ref mut bytes: MutSpan[u8])`: the call `len=bytes.len()` gives an int to a usize field. That is not a coercion (p04-types.md 63-74, rule 1 has no i64 to u64), so as written it is E2020, and it needs `bytes.len() as usize`. Reach of the edit at depth: a struct field holding a struct with a fixed array of raw pointers (refused); Span[*c_char] argv elements (refused, and accepted today, so the edit closes a second route nobody had listed); an opaque type behind a contracted pointer (not reached); a POD C++ class's method object (refused); a `ref mut` result view into C memory (refused, which is needed); a union member (refused by 'a field ... at any depth', nothing new).

All three were there before the edit, and they refute the edit's ODR-075 line ('closes the one route').

outs.notes:
Engineering lens, read-only. Nothing was run, and every outcome is from the part files' text. Verdict: broken. Two medium holes are caused by the edit itself.

Hole 1, results. The edit refuses raw pointers in copies C hands to safe code: a by-value result, an `out one` value, a read-only view. SDL_GetCurrentDisplayMode is the example. Safe code cannot use such a pointer without `unsafe`, and ODR-073's ruling is about passing a pointer from safe code. Widening ODR-073 here is a choice the edit records as no choice ("decided", decisions []). By D2's order, C2 comes before C6.

Hole 3, function types. "Held anywhere in one's Ember type" leaves function-pointer types undecided: the wide reading refuses FFI-52's own example and qsort-style comparators; the narrow one lets a callback's raw-pointer result through (hole 5).

One property fixes both: judge a raw pointer by direction. It is refused where its value flows from safe code to what C reads: an input; C memory that safe code may write through a `ref mut` view or an `owns` value; an Ember function's result given to C. It is not refused in what C hands to safe code. The edit already gets the `ref mut` result view right (test k07_ref_mut_result_view_into_c_memory_refused, which compiles today and over-reads), so the result half is needed there and only there.

Hole 2 (low): handle typedefs are judged by how they are represented, and per target, while the notes say they are K46's.

Holes 4 to 6 were there before the edit; they are new gaps for the list. They also refute the edit's ODR-075 line ("closes the one route"): an unsafe function value in a field, an Ember callback's result, and a safe field write into an adopted owns T that C's destructor reads.

Edit-input findings that are not spec holes:
(a) The answer's wrapper `len=bytes.len()` is E2020, because int to usize is not a coercion (p04 63-74). The tests use `bytes.len() as usize`.
(b) Sibling 2's extend wrapper needs a raw pointer from a CStrView, and FFI-15 (p16 369-381) gives none. The test uses Span.as_ptr (SPN-8) over an Array with a NUL instead.
(c) Whether sibling 3's `fn mixer_get_default()` (a function-pointer result with no nullability word) is accepted is not settled by FFI-1 today.

existing_rule.words: A raw `*T` can be declared for an unsafe call, but complete facts do not make a raw-pointer parameter or result safe to expose; `safe fn` with one is `E5002`. (Recorded as ODR-073, p26-appx-h.md 361, whose ruling reads: "complete `@ffi` facts alone never make that raw pointer safe to pass from Safe code", docs/OWNER-QUEUE.md 3682-3684, chosen because "a safe caller may pass a null, dangling or forged pointer", 3672-3673.)

One held in what C only hands to safe code is allowed: reading through it is unsafe. Every declaration asserting foreign code safe to call keeps to this or, naming where the pointer is held and the line to write, is
edits.why_general: This is FFI-10's own property, in ODR-073's ruling words: complete facts never make a raw pointer "safe to pass from Safe code", because safe code can set one to any address (`ref_to_ptr`, `as_ptr()`, `null[P]()` are safe, §IV.5, SPN-8). The edit judges the property by which way the value goes, not by where it sits in a type. So one set of words covers every type (struct, union, enum payload, fixed array, span element, the value a contracted pointer views), every route into C (an argument, a method's object, a callback's result, C memory that safe code may write through a `ref mut` or `MutSpan` result, the field an `owns` value's destructor reads), and every declaration that asserts foreign code safe (a hand `safe fn`, a C or C++ overlay entry, an `@ffi(safe)` typedef, an `@ffi(std_function)` type), without naming any of them. What C only hands to safe code (a copied result's fields, an `out` value, a callback's parameters) is left alone, because reading through a raw pointer already needs `unsafe` (§IV.5). The rule for a raw-pointer parameter or result itself is kept word for word.

edits.after: scalar or a `@layout(c)` value type that `[FFI-10]` allows (`E5002` otherwise)
edits.why_general: FFI-56's list is FFI-10's list applied to C function pointers. Pointing it at FFI-10's rule keeps the two lists from contradicting each other. A call through an asserted typedef can then not hand C a raw pointer that safe code set in a parameter's struct, and a struct the pointer returns is judged as any result C hands to safe code.

out.notes:
The one repair round. The outcome stays `decided`. FFI-10's property, in ODR-073's ruling ("complete `@ffi` facts alone never make that raw pointer safe to pass from Safe code", docs/OWNER-QUEUE.md 3682-3684, chosen because "a safe caller may pass a null, dangling or forged pointer"), is about a raw pointer going from safe code to C. The first answer judged where a raw pointer sits in a type instead. That refused copies C hands to safe code (E1-1, an ordinary SDL call) and left callback types to the reader (S1-6, E1-2).

The repair states the direction once. A raw pointer is refused where C reads it and safe code may have set it: at any depth of an argument or a method's object, in what an Ember function given to C returns, or in a result safe code may write (`ref mut`, `MutSpan`, `owns`, which C reads again). It is allowed in what C only hands to safe code.

The rule for a raw-pointer parameter or result itself is kept word for word, so ODR-073's result half is neither reversed nor widened: a direct `-> *u8` stays E5002, while a struct C fills and hands back compiles. No new choice is made. Not refusing C's copies is what the ruling's words say, and refusing them would widen ODR-073 to fields.

Pre-existing gaps the breakers found, for the list and not repaired here:
(1) An `unsafe extern "C" fn` value that safe code puts in a struct field C calls (S1-2, E1-4). This is an unvouched precondition, not a raw pointer.
(2) A raw-pointer field of a foreign value that C reads later, rewritten by safe code after `adopt` (S1-4, E1-6). This is outside FFI-10, which judges declarations; it would need field writes to such values to be unsafe.
(3) Whether an `@ffi(newtype)` over a C pointer counts as a raw pointer (S1-5), together with K46.

The repaired words also close two pre-existing routes as a consequence of the property, with no clause for either: a callback that returns a raw pointer to C (S1-1, E1-5), and an `@ffi(std_function)` entry whose parameter holds one (S1-3).

Corrections to the first answer:
- Pointer-represented handles are reached by their type: a `Span` of them going to C is refused, rightly (E1-3). A 32-bit `uint64_t` handle is a scalar, which FFI-2 already treats as asserted.
- ODR-075's route is not fully closed (gap 2).
- The `line to write` for a hand declaration is its raw C ABI form (p16-ffi.md 91-92); the message words are the lead's.

The XVI.4 Vulkan example becomes E5002 and is rewritten once with K46 (J8-14). `ref_to_ptr(ref mut x)` follows K51 (J2-11).

The new text was kept shorter than the first answer's by eye; the script measures it. The start-up reading (AUTOPILOT, HANDOFF) was skipped, as the task says. Nothing was run; every claim needing the compiler is in to_verify. The relayed request to hibernate the laptop is for the main session after the workflow, not this step, and was not acted on here.

triage.evidence: Today `safe fn netq_drain(next_buffer: extern "C" fn(usize) -> *mut u8, want: usize)` passes FFI-10's list (p16-ffi.md 59-61, "a pointer whose contract is complete", with the callback contract of 400-405). Lines 82-84 refuse only "a raw-pointer parameter or result". Returning `ref_to_ptr` of a local is safe (p04-types.md 340-345), and FFI-21a refuses only a pointer into a parameter's copy (p16-ffi.md 428-431). So the same program writes through a dangling stack pointer without the edit. It is a new gap, not this edit's; the repaired words reach it anyway ("what an Ember function given to C returns").

`job.run` imports as `unsafe extern "C" fn(usize)` (p16-ffi.md 590-592), and an `unsafe fn` coerces to that type (p05-declarations.md 183: "an `unsafe fn` coerces only to an `unsafe` callable type"); only calling it is unsafe. `job` holds no raw pointer, so the program frees address 4096 today, with or without the edit. An unvouched function value handed to C is a related but different property from a raw pointer. New gap for the list.

p21-annex-c.md 67: with `@ffi(std_function)`, a `std::function` is "a function value of type `fn(A…) -> R` … called as any other". Nothing checks its parameter types today, a direct `float*` included, so it overflows without the edit. The repaired "Every declaration asserting foreign code safe to call" reaches that entry, since an `unsafe overlay` entry is an assertion (p16-ffi.md 278-281). Its `Block` parameter is then refused by the same property.

`adopt` is an `unsafe fn`, vouched for the blob as made (p16-ffi.md 386-389). Afterwards `second.data = first.data` is safe, because p04-types.md 345-346 makes only "Dereferencing, offsetting, reading and writing through it" unsafe. The ends call `blob_free` (599-601). It double-frees today in exactly this way. The repaired edit refuses the `returns_owned` form (an `owns` result safe code may write). The field write after `adopt` is outside FFI-10, which judges declarations: new gap.

Whether an `@ffi(newtype)` over a C pointer (p16-ffi.md 185: "a nominal type with the typedef's representation, … converted with `as` only") counts as a raw pointer is already open today for a direct parameter. Whether `null[*mut tex]() as tex_ref` is safe is not settled by p04-types.md 345-347, which names raw-to-raw and pointer/integer casts. It is the same before and after the edit, and goes with K46 (what a handle-like type is).

The first edit's "held anywhere in one's Ember type" reads naturally as reaching a callable type's parameter types, and its bracket (field, element, payload, pointee) does not exclude them. On that reading, the FFI-21 run-pass test with `pick: extern "C" fn(*mut void, *mut void) -> c_int`, where C hands both pointers to Ember, is refused. This is caused by the edit's wording (cause C1).

Under the edit, XVI.4's `vkCreateBuffer(device: borrowed, pCreateInfo: borrowed one, pAllocator: nullable borrowed one, pBuffer: out one)` (p16-ffi.md 239-241) is E5002. C reads `VkBufferCreateInfo.pNext`, `.pQueueFamilyIndices` and `VkAllocationCallbacks.pUserData`, which safe code may set. That is J8-08's danger in the spec's own example (cause C2). The example is outside the allowed rules and is rewritten once with K46.

FFI-10 already gives the unsafe line: "An unsafe raw-pointer declaration keeps its written C ABI parameters; only a mapped `safe fn` erases the witness" (p16-ffi.md 91-92), and "An unsafe raw declaration keeps its written count parameter" (109-110). So the line that compiles is `unsafe fn writev(fd: c_int, iov: *IoVec, iovcnt: c_int) -> isize` with `@safety` above it. A message's words are the lead's (JOB.md 1261-1263), bound by "the exact line to write instead" (JOB.md 1269-1270). The repaired words say "the line to write", which covers a typedef too (drop `@ffi(safe)`).

Under the first edit, "or a result, or held anywhere in one's Ember type (… also in what a contracted pointer points to)" reaches `mode: out one`'s value, so `SDL_GetCurrentDisplayMode` is refused for `SDL_DisplayMode.driverdata`. Nothing in the program can break memory safety: reading through `driverdata` needs `unsafe` (p04-types.md 345-346), and handing the struct back to C is an argument, refused by the input half. ODR-073's ruling says "safe to pass from Safe code" (docs/OWNER-QUEUE.md 3683-3684). A correct ordinary game call is refused: caused by the edit (cause C1).

Same wording as S1-6. On the wide reading, `cmp: extern "C" fn(*i32, *i32) -> c_int` and FFI-52's own `safe fn register_cb(cb: extern "C" fn(*mut void), ud: *mut void)` (p16-ffi.md 492-493) are refused. On the narrow reading, the words say nothing about a callback's result. Two compilers written from these words could disagree. Caused by the edit (cause C1).

Refusing `pBuffers`, a `Span[VkBuffer]` whose elements are `*mut VkBuffer_T` on a 64-bit target (p16-ffi.md 183, 185), is the property's correct outcome. Safe code can fill the span with `null[*mut vk.VkBuffer_T]()` (safe, p04-types.md 347) or a destroyed buffer, which the driver dereferences. An element can carry no contract word (p16-ffi.md 210-211). The same type as a direct parameter with no contract is refused today too (82-84), so element and parameter are judged alike. On a 32-bit target `VkBuffer` is `uint64_t`, a scalar, which FFI-2 already treats as asserted (p16-ffi.md 35-36, "a scalar can be an address"): that is pre-existing. What `@ffi(handle)` makes a handle's type is K46's question, and the element rule follows that type. `pBuffer: out one` is C handing the handle to Ember, which the repaired words do not refuse. The first answer's note that handles were not reached was wrong and is corrected.

Same as S1-2. `reap: unsafe extern "C" fn(usize)` holds no raw pointer, and `free_addr` coerces to it in safe code (p05-declarations.md 182-185). It corrupts the heap today, with or without the edit. New gap: an unvouched `unsafe` function value handed to C.

Same as S1-1: it compiles and writes through a dangling stack pointer today (p05-declarations.md 185-186, p16-ffi.md 424-434). It is not caused by the edit, and the repaired words reach it ("what an Ember function given to C returns"). The first answer's claim that ODR-075's route was closed is withdrawn.

Same as S1-4. `adopt` inside `unsafe:`, then `canvas.pixels = ref_to_ptr(ref mut stray)`, is safe today (p04-types.md 340-346), and `SDL_FreeSurface` at the end frees a stack byte (p16-ffi.md 386-389, 599-601). It is not caused by the edit and is outside FFI-10, since no declaration asserts it: new gap.

causes.cause: C1: the first edit judged a raw pointer by where it sits in a type, but FFI-10's property is about which way it goes. Its reason, and ODR-073's ruling ("never make that raw pointer safe to pass from Safe code", docs/OWNER-QUEUE.md 3683-3684, over the option where "a safe caller may pass a null, dangling or forged pointer"), is a raw pointer that safe code may have set reaching what C reads. Judged by position, the words refused copies C hands to safe code (E1-1) and left a callable type's parameters and result to the reader (S1-6, E1-2). The repair states the direction once: refused where C reads a raw pointer safe code may have set, at any depth and by any route; allowed where C only hands one to safe code.

C2: the spec's own model overlay (XVI.4) asserts safe a call whose argument values hold raw pointers C reads. The property is right to refuse it. The example lies outside the allowed rules, so it is rewritten once with K46 (J8-14), not by this edit.

I tested the repaired edit with the safety lens. Nothing was run; every outcome comes from the part files.

Verdict: the edit tightens safety and loosens nothing. Its one allowance, a raw pointer held in what C only hands to safe code, was already accepted before the edit. FFI-56 as edited is the same as before or stricter. The edit is still broken, because two medium holes are caused by its new last sentence ("Every declaration asserting foreign code safe to call keeps to this or, naming ... the line to write, is E5002"):

- **Hole 1.** The sentence does not say whether `@ffi(destroys(f))` on a struct type is such a declaration.
  - If it is, the asset loader's own fix line does not compile, and every owned foreign struct that holds a pointer (SDL_Surface) is refused with no line to write.
  - If it is not, the `returns_owned` refusal protects nothing: one safe field write after `adopt` gives the same double free.
  - So the repair's note that this route lies "outside FFI-10, which judges declarations" does not hold: `destroys(f)` is a declaration.
- **Hole 5.** The sentence reaches `@ffi(std_function)`, as the edit intends, but the language has no unsafe form of a `std::function` value. A correct C++-interop program is refused with no line that compiles (checklist 9 and 12).
- **Hole 4.** S1-7 (XVI.4 vkCreateBuffer) still stands. It is low, and the edit rightly defers it to K46.

Triage re-test of the first round's holes:
- **Repaired, confirmed:** S1-6, E1-1 and E1-2. The direction wording keeps callback parameters, out values and C's copies accepted.
- **Correctly pre_existing:** S1-1, S1-2, S1-3, S1-4, S1-5, E1-4, E1-5 and E1-6. Without the edit each goes wrong the same way. The repaired words now close S1-1, E1-5 and S1-3; S1-3's refusal is what exposes hole 5.

New pre-existing gaps for the list:
- **Hole 2.** An Ember override of a C++ virtual returns, from safe code, a raw pointer that C++ reads. The same goes for an `@unsafe(export)` function's result.
- **Hole 3.** An Ember function written into C memory through a `ref mut` result's function-pointer field. The edit's words combine two routes it names without saying whether the combination is reached.

Smaller points:
- **to_verify item 3 is wrong as written.** It expects "no W3012", but the answer's "after" `unsafe extern \"C\":` block has no `# SAFETY:` note, so it draws W3012 (p09-memory.md 331-335). My test adds the note.

holes.today: Compiles and prints `ran 3 frames`. The entry asserts the call safe (p16-ffi.md 278-281). Its result `borrowed one exclusive from(static)` is a `ref mut frame_input` (p16-ffi.md 291, 293-294, 104-105 ODR-078). The accepted test tests/conformance/FFI-11/accept_exclusive_one_nullable_static_result.em has the same shape. Lines 82-84 refuse only a raw-pointer parameter or result. The loop writes three `f32` fields and never touches a pointer field.
holes.with_edit: E5002 at `fn engine_input`, naming `frame_input.ini_path` and `frame_input.user_data`, because the result is one "safe code may write (`ref mut`, ...)" that holds raw pointers (p16-ffi.md 83 as edited). The line to write is `@safety("…")` above `unsafe fn engine_input()`, which gives a raw `*mut frame_input`. Each frame's three scalar writes then go through the raw pointer inside `unsafe:` (p04-types.md 345-346). The other way is for the binding to grow one setter wrapper per field, because no word can describe a field (FFI-30a, p16-ffi.md 210-212).
holes.what_goes_wrong: An ordinary game loop is refused for a line it does not contain: `input.ini_path = ref_to_ptr(ref mut b)`. The danger lives at the write of a pointer field, not at the declaration that gives the view. So every program that takes a writable view of a C struct with any pointer field pays: ImGui's IO block every frame, a window surface, a stream state. The rare dangerous line is what should pay. The edit's readability verdict ("Only a binding that hands C a raw pointer which safe code may set changes") misses these programs. Refusing the view, rather than the pointer-field write, is a choice, and it is made with `decisions: []` under outcome `decided`.
holes.fix_hint: Judge the raw pointer where safe code sets it: writing a raw-pointer field of C memory (through a `ref mut`/`MutSpan` view or a foreign `owns` value) needs `unsafe`, as writing through a raw pointer does, and the declaration giving the view is not refused.

holes.today: Compiles and prints the splash size (or `no splash`). `path` is a `CStrView` (p16-ffi.md 291, 377-381). The result is an `Option` of an `owns image` whose end calls `image_free` (p16-ffi.md 290, 386-390, 599-601). Lines 82-84 reach neither. The program only reads scalar fields.
holes.with_edit: E5002 at `fn image_load`, naming `image.pixels`: an `owns` result "safe code may write" (p16-ffi.md 83 as edited). The line to write, as in the edit's asset-loader case, is `@safety("the caller ends the result once, with `image_free`")` above `unsafe fn image_load(path)`, with `adopt[im.image]` inside `unsafe:` (p16-ffi.md 386-389), usually in an `extend` wrapper (FFI-13, 356-357). That wrapper returns the same `owns image`. So `splash.pixels = ref_to_ptr(ref mut b)` is still safe code, and `image_free` still frees a stack byte. The edit's own sibling outcome concedes this ("The same field write after `adopt` stays possible").
holes.what_goes_wrong: A correct loader that only reads `width` and `height` is refused. The rewrite the message gives then restores exactly the danger the refusal names: an invalid free, `free` on a pointer the program never allocated. Every `returns_owned` binding of a C struct with a pointer field (an image, a JSON node, a font face) gains a wrapper and no safety. The pointer-field write is the one place the edit's property ('safe code may have set') can actually be enforced for an owned foreign value.
holes.fix_hint: The same property as hole 1: setting a raw-pointer field of an owned foreign value, or of C memory reached through a view, needs `unsafe`, so the `owns` result is not refused and the adopt route is closed too.

holes.today: Compiles and prints `2`. `better` has a complete callback contract (p16-ffi.md 400-405). `closer` is capture-free and coerces to `extern "C" fn` (p05-declarations.md 185-186). It returns one of the pointers C passed it, which is the form FFI-21a itself prescribes: "A function that must give C back a pointer it was given takes that parameter as a pointer (`*T`)" (p16-ffi.md 433-434). It is not E5042, because the pointer is not into a by-value copy (424-432).
holes.with_edit: E5002 at `safe fn ai_best_id`, naming `better`'s result, because "what an Ember function given to C returns" holds a raw pointer (p16-ffi.md 83 as edited). The callable type is judged, whatever function is given.
holes.what_goes_wrong: The compiler already reads the body of every function given to C: FFI-21a follows a returned pointer "through copies, conversions and aggregates" to refuse one into a parameter's copy. Here it could see that `closer` returns only pointers C passed it. The edit judges the type instead, so FFI-21a's own pattern can no longer be used with a safe declaration, and the programmer writes `unsafe fn` plus a wrapper for a fact the compiler can work out (principle 1, verdict 137's lesson).
holes.rule_lines: p16-ffi.md 83 (FFI-10 as edited), 400-405 (FFI-21), 424-434 (FFI-21a); p05-declarations.md 185-186
holes.fix_hint: Judge what an Ember function given to C returns from its body, as FFI-21a does: a raw pointer C passed it goes back; one safe code made (`ref_to_ptr`, `as_ptr()`, `null`) is refused where it is returned.

holes.today: Compiles. FFI-31b's list of what may not appear in an export does not include a raw pointer (p16-ffi.md 647-651). FFI-21a refuses only a pointer into a by-value parameter's copy, and `byte` is a local (424-434). `ref_to_ptr(ref mut byte)` is safe (p04-types.md 340-342). The export's `# SAFETY:` note vouches for the symbol only (622-636). The host writes through a dangling stack pointer: a use after return.
holes.with_edit: Unchanged. "What an Ember function given to C returns" could be read to reach an export, but the refusal falls only on "Every declaration asserting foreign code safe to call", and an export is no such declaration. So it still compiles. The same holds for an `@export_table` field and for a C++ override that C++ calls (p21-annex-c.md 121-125, 147-155).
holes.what_goes_wrong: The edit's own direction property (a raw pointer that safe code made, read by C) has other routes into C that no declaration covers: every way FFI-52 lists for C to reach an Ember function besides a declaration's callback argument. This is a new gap for the list, not this edit's.
holes.fix_hint: Judge every Ember function C can call (export, table field, override, callback) by the one direction: a raw pointer it returns to C that safe code made is refused where it is returned.

holes.today: Run-pass, stdout `25 4.5 7 7 true false`, with L3015 for `PAIR_FIRST` (the test's own header, lines 1-8). The raw parameter leaves a fact unknown, so the call requires `unsafe` (FFI-2, p16-ffi.md 33-34). Lines 82-84 refuse a raw pointer only on a hand `safe fn`. FFI-11c treats a `TODO(count)` pointer the same way: the entry stays and its calls stay unsafe (p16-ffi.md 318-321).
holes.with_edit: The refusal's subject changes from "`safe fn` with one" to "Every declaration asserting foreign code safe to call keeps to this or ... is E5002". A function entry "asserts the function safe to call" (GRM-35, p16-ffi.md 278-280). On that reading, `fn PAIR_FIRST(p: *Pair) -> i64` is E5002, the run-pass test fails, and so does every overlay entry holding a `TODO(count)` pointer. On FFI-2's reading (an unknown fact makes the call unsafe), the entry "keeps to this" and compiles. The words do not say which. The edit claims that the raw-pointer rule "is kept word for word" and that no test is newly refused.
holes.what_goes_wrong: An existing conformance test, and FFI-11c's day-one path ("A header can be adopted on the first day with everything behind `unsafe:`, and made safe one function at a time"), change outcome or become undecided. This happens outside the question and with no recorded decision. Two compilers built from these words disagree on an ordinary overlay. Refusing such entries in favour of `unsafe fn` may be what verdicts 130 and 136 point to, but that is a choice reaching FFI-2 and FFI-11c, not one this edit can make silently.
holes.rule_lines: p16-ffi.md 82-84 (FFI-10 as edited), 33-42 (FFI-2), 277-282 (GRM-35), 318-321 (FFI-11c); tests/conformance/FFI-6b/accept_a_declared_macro_is_called_through_its_wrapper.em 1-23; tests/conformance/FFI-6b/overlays/macros.em 11-12

existing_rule.words: THR-8: "A type is **`Send`** when a value of it may be handed over to another thread ... an `owns T` when `T` is; ... `dyn I` when `I` requires it (`interface I: needs Send:`)." ERR-3: "`Error` is the interface of error types: `Display + Debug` with `fn source() ...`" (p04 676: `interface Error: needs (Debug, Display):`, no Send). ERR-8: AnyError is "a `dyn Error` held alone (`owns dyn Error`)" implementing "`From[E]` for every `E: needs Error`". THR-10: "`R` MUST be `Send` (`E7015`, `E7008`)". IFC-3: "a bound brings its parents". Together they decide today, with no one having chosen it, that AnyError is not Send, so the worker is refused at spawn. The compiler cannot tell what an erased error holds; THR-8's own clause for a dyn already says how an erased value is made safe for threads: by what its interface requires. The choice is whether that requirement sits on what an error is, or on the catch-all's conversion.

edits.before: `Display + Debug` with `fn source() -> Option[ref dyn Error]` (default `None`) (§IV.8).
edits.after: `interface Error: needs (Debug, Display, Send, ThreadShared):` with `fn source() -> Option[ref dyn Error]` (default `None`) (§IV.8), so any thread may have and read every error, `dyn Error` and `AnyError` (`[THR-8]`). A type that is not `Send` and `ThreadShared` is `E2040` where it implements `Error`, the message naming what in it is not and the words to write (`[THR-2]`).
edits.why_general: It states the property on what an error is: any thread may have and read it. Every place that names an error then carries it with nothing written: a bound `E: needs Error` or `type Failure: needs Error` (a bound brings its parents, IFC-3 p05 411-413), a field `owns dyn Error`, and AnyError itself (THR-8's existing clause: a dyn is Send when its interface requires it). So every route is covered at once: a thread's result, a channel element, a job's data, a thread_shared holder, an RwLock, a `ref` given to a scoped task. The refusal sits where a type is made an error, the one place its contents are known, and the marker rules decide it for every one-thread part (a shares owner, a weakref link, a sharedref mut link, a Cell) with no list of cases. ERR-1's "any `E: needs Error`", ERR-8's `From` and ERR-9's "any error" stay true as written. The parents are spelled with `needs`, as verdict 110 spells them.

edits.before: `dyn I` when `I` requires it (`interface I: needs Send:`).
edits.after: `dyn I` when `I` requires it (`interface I: needs Send:`), as it is `ThreadShared` when `I` requires that (ODR-255).
edits.why_general: THR-9 says ThreadShared is inferred like Send but no rule says it for a dyn. ODR-255 already ruled that a dyn is Send and Sync (now ThreadShared) by what its interface requires. The words now say so for every interface, a program's own (`interface Command: needs (Send, ThreadShared):`) as well as Error. There is no second spelling: the markers go in the interface's `needs`, never after `dyn` with `+`.

answers.today: Refused at the `h = thread.spawn(...)` line, and the text never says so in words. `R` is `Result[int, AnyError]`, which must be Send (THR-10, p11 176). AnyError holds `owns dyn Error` (ERR-8, p13 94). `dyn Error` is Send only when Error requires Send (THR-8, p11 51), and Error requires only Debug and Display (ERR-3, p13 88; p04 676). The code is E7015 or E7008 (THR-10 names both). What the compiler does today is listed in to_verify. The danger the refusal guards against, in C++ terms: an exception object holding a non-atomic reference-counted pointer, rethrown on another thread through std::exception_ptr, so two threads race on the count.

import std.fs
import std.io
import std.thread

fn load(path: StrView) -> Result[int, io.Error]:   # a concrete error type, written only so the result may cross threads
    text = fs.read_to_string(path)?
    return Ok(text.len())

fn main() -> Result[void]:
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() => load("level1.cfg"))
    n = h.join()?                                   # io.Error -> AnyError here
    println(n)
    return Ok(())

# with a second kind of failure (a parse step), the worker also needs an @derive(Error) enum with an @from variant for each kind
readability.verdict: The after is shorter (no `import std.io`, no concrete error type) and reads like the one-thread program. With two kinds of failure it also saves a whole error enum. It adds no word anywhere. Generic error code (`type Failure: needs Error`) and error wrappers holding `owns dyn Error` stay exactly as today, where option A made them grow `needs (Send, ThreadShared)` and `+ Send + ThreadShared`. The cost falls only on an error type holding a one-thread part, which is refused at its own declaration with the words to write.

final.cost: Compile time: Send and ThreadShared are inferred, and are checked once, where a type implements Error. A `?` into AnyError is checked as today. Run time: AnyError keeps its layout (the boxed error's data and table pointers, its identity, the context list) and its one allocation on the failure path (ERR-11). A `?` into it costs what it costs today, and the success path costs nothing, as in C. Handing an AnyError to another thread runs verdict 114's hand-over check on what its error owns (THR-2 p11 119-121) through the error's table: one indirect call per AnyError handed over, then one compare for each object it owns whose class has weakref links. Nothing runs in a program where no class has weakref links. C pays nothing to pass an error pointer to another thread. To measure: AnyError's size and failure-path time against today's build, and the time of that hand-over check.

verdicts_kept.how: Kept. The same marker rules decide which types may be errors, so an error holding such a link is refused where it implements Error.

verdicts_kept.verdict: 165 (thread_shared refused where the value is made when something in it is not ThreadShared)
verdicts_kept.how: Kept, and the choice follows its shape: the refusal is where a type is made an error, not where an error later reaches a thread. A thread_shared object holding errors passes that check.

verdicts_kept.verdict: 166 (a scoped task neither makes nor ends a shares owner)
verdicts_kept.how: Kept. No error holds a shares owner, so making or ending an error in a scoped task touches no one-thread count.

decisions.title: Where an error that only one thread may have is refused: where its type is declared an error, where it goes into the catch-all error, or where it leaves the thread
decisions.problem: AnyError erases its error's type, so the compiler cannot tell whether a given AnyError holds an error with a one-thread part. Today's rules make AnyError unsafe to send, by accident and with no choice ever made. So an ordinary worker returning `Result[int]` is refused at `thread.spawn`, and the text never says so. Something must refuse the one-thread error somewhere. The first answer put the check on the catch-all's conversion (A). The breakers showed that A also makes ordinary generic error code and error wrappers write thread words, makes the rules that say 'any error' untrue, and needs a new `dyn I + Send` spelling with no conversion rule behind it.

options.code:
## std.core
pub struct AnyError:
    error: owns dyn Error + Send + ThreadShared
    ...
extend[E: needs (Error, Send, ThreadShared)] AnyError implements From[E]:
    ...
## a generic library
[S: needs Source]
pub fn count_lines(src: S) -> Result[int] where S.Failure: needs (Send, ThreadShared):
    text = src.read_all()?
## an error wrapper
struct ImportError:
    cause: owns dyn Error + Send + ThreadShared
options.outcome: The worker compiles. A one-thread error is refused at its `?` into AnyError (E2040), even with one thread. Generic code whose error is only `needs Error` must also write `where S.Failure: needs (Send, ThreadShared)`. A wrapper holding `owns dyn Error` must write `owns dyn Error + Send + ThreadShared`, which is a second spelling of the markers, and its `source()` then needs a conversion the spec does not have. ERR-1's 'any `E: needs Error`' and ERR-9's 'any error' become untrue.

Today's rules. The `Result[int]` worker is refused at the spawn line (E7015). A worker must name a concrete error type: an @derive(Error) enum with an @from variant per kind when it can fail two ways, converted after join.

options.code:
## std unchanged; the compiler collects every error type converted into AnyError anywhere in the program
fn load(path: StrView) -> Result[int]:
    ...
h = thread.spawn(owns fn() => load("level1.cfg"))
options.outcome: The worker compiles until some `?` anywhere in the program, even in code that never meets a thread, puts a one-thread error into an AnyError. From then on every spawn, channel or thread_shared holder of AnyError is refused, with a message naming that distant line. This is the whole-program search that verdict 61 turned down for function values.

The worker compiles. Generic error code (`needs Error`) and wrappers holding `owns dyn Error` compile with nothing written, and every rule that says 'any error' stays true. An error type holding a one-thread part (a shares owner, a weakref link to a one-thread value, a sharedref mut link, a Cell) is refused where it implements Error (E2040, with the words to write), even if it never leaves its thread. One holding a raw pointer is refused until its author may vouch for ThreadShared, which is the pending vouching question (P04, J7-06); A refused the same error at its `?`. This is Swift's choice: its Error refines Sendable.

options.code:
pub struct AnyError:
    error: owns dyn Error + Send
extend[E: needs (Error, Send)] AnyError implements From[E]:
options.outcome: The worker compiles. AnyError is Send but not ThreadShared, so `assets = thread_shared Assets()` holding `RwLock[Array[Result[Texture]]]` is refused at its line (verdict 165), and a `ref` to an AnyError cannot go to scoped tasks. It has A's costs for Send: generic bounds and dyn fields must name it.

decisions.parameters_in_order: 1. The three goals at once. B fails 'Python-like', because the ordinary worker grows a concrete error type and an enum per kind. A and E fail it for ordinary library and error-wrapping code, which grows thread words (holes E1-1, E1-2). C and D keep all of it as today. 2. Safety (C4): every option refuses before a one-thread value crosses. A's safety for program-defined erased types also rested on a conversion to `dyn I + Send` that no rule states (hole S1-2); D needs no such conversion. 3. Compile time first (C5): all are decided when compiling. Each adds only verdict 114's existing hand-over check, through a table, when an AnyError crosses (stated in cost). 4. A written word only for meaning (C3): A writes `needs (Send, ThreadShared)` in generic bounds and `+ Send + ThreadShared` on dyn fields, words that say nothing the program does (bookkeeping). B writes a concrete error type. C and D write nothing. 5. Ordinary program no longer or harder (C2): C lets an edit anywhere break a spawn far away. D refuses only an error type holding a one-thread part, at its own line with the words to write. These are the same errors A refused at their `?`, which nearly every error reaches since main returns AnyError, plus the rare one that never leaves its thread. 6. Consistency (C6): D uses THR-8's existing clause (a dyn is Send by what its interface requires) and ODR-255, IFC-3 (a bound brings its parents), verdict 110's `needs` spelling, verdict 61 (the type says which threads may have it), verdict 165 (refused where it is made), no `+` (verdict 109; decisions.md line 141 left `+` after dyn unanswered), and Swift's Error: Sendable. It keeps ERR-1, ERR-8 and ERR-9 true as written. So D.
decisions.departs_from_verdict: none. Verdict 110 settled how Error's parents are spelled (`needs (Debug, Display)`); this keeps that spelling and adds two parents to the list, which no verdict decided.
decisions.recommendation: D: every error type may go to and be read by any thread, checked where the type is declared an error. The catch-all error, generic error code and error wrappers then need no word, and only an error type holding a one-thread part is refused, at its own line with the words to write. Present it with the pending ThreadShared vouch (P04, J7-06), which decides the raw-pointer error.

owner_short.one_line: C++ analogue: should every exception type be required to be safe to hand to and read from any thread, so that a catch-all holder like std::exception_ptr can always cross threads?
owner_short.step_table:
| step | who | what happens | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | an error type's author | declares an error holding plain values (a code, a text) | allowed: it may go to any thread |
| 2 | worker thread | `fs.read_to_string(path)?` puts the file error into the catch-all error | allowed, nothing written |
| 3 | worker thread | returns `Result[int]` (count or catch-all error) from the thread | allowed: every error may go to any thread |
| 4 | main thread | `n = h.join()?` | gets the count, or passes the error on |
| 5 | an error type's author | declares an error holding a one-thread shared owner | refused when compiling at that declaration, with the line to write |
owner_short.today: The worker returning `Result[int]` is refused at `thread.spawn` without the text saying so; it must name a concrete error type instead.
options: A: the catch-all error is safe for every thread and checks each error where `?` puts it in; generic error code and error wrappers must then add thread words
B: keep today: the catch-all stays on its thread; a worker names its own error type, an enum when it can fail two ways
C: the compiler searches the whole program; one one-thread error put in anywhere makes every thread hand-off of the catch-all fail, far from that line
D: every error type is safe for every thread (as Swift's errors are), checked where the error type is declared; nothing is written anywhere else
E: the catch-all may be sent but not read by two threads at once; a shared cache of load results is refused
owner_short.recommendation: D: ordinary worker, library and error-wrapping code compile with nothing written; only an error type holding a one-thread part is refused, at its own declaration with the fix (one holding a raw pointer waits on the pending question of vouching for thread sharing).

final.notes: Repair of the first answer: option A (ERR-8's two changes and THR-8's `dyn I + Send` words) is withdrawn and replaced by option D, an ERR-3 change plus a short THR-8 addition, both allowed rules. ERR-1 (p13 46-47), ERR-8 (p13 93-95) and ERR-9 (p13 48-49) need no change and stay true. The one text that must follow is the declaration ERR-3 cites. p04-types.md line 676 (§IV.8's `interface Error: needs (Debug, Display):`) and std/src/core.em line 80 must read `needs (Debug, Display, Send, ThreadShared)`. This is the same declaration copied, not a second rule, but until the lead writes it the sketch disagrees with ERR-3. ERR-3's prose had the old `Display + Debug` spelling; the new words use verdict 110's. The ThreadShared clause for a dyn is placed in THR-8 because THR-9 is not an allowed rule; ODR-255 already ruled it. Cause 3 (holes S1-3, E1-5) is not answered by this edit: ThreadShared cannot be vouched (TYP-43 p04 592-594), which is group P04's pending question (J7-06). Until it is answered, an error holding a raw pointer cannot be an Error under D (under A it could not go into AnyError), so present the two together. Pre-existing gaps for the list, not changed here: S1-4 (THR-15 makes channel ends Send whatever their element; lead fix J7-07) and E1-7 (the grammar's `dyn` bound list p03 72/171 has no meaning and TYP-5 rule 8 converts to one interface). Under D nothing depends on E1-7. Possible further gap, there before this edit: whether an error may hold a view of a place (Rust's 'static bound on anyhow). The importer program from E1-2 lacked `from std.fmt import Formatter, FmtError`; it is added in the sibling, and this does not change the finding. Per memory, an in-place edit to a cut hardening may only add text; this changes meaning, so the lead places it in a new hardening. Nothing was run; docs/AUTOPILOT.md and HANDOFF.md were skipped, as the workflow says review agents should. The relayed request to hibernate the laptop is for the orchestrator after the workflow, not for this step, so it was not acted on here.

triage.evidence: The edited ERR-8 (p13 95) bounds `From[E]` by `E: needs (Error, Send, ThreadShared)`, while ERR-1 (p13 46-47) still says "converting one into `AnyError` takes any `E: needs Error`". The spec then decides `n = parse_header(file)?` both ways. ERR-2 (p13 51-52) routes `?` through `F.from`, so the race needs ERR-1's reading, but the contradiction is the edit's: without it the two rules agree. Cause 1.

With the edit, THR-8 (p11 51) makes `dyn Command + Send` Send, so the spawn's safety rests on refusing `owns Clear(palette=...)` into it. TYP-5 rule 8 (p04 84-86) converts only to "an interface its type implements", and no rule or code refuses that line. Today THR-8 does not make that type Send, so the spawn is refused whatever the conversion does. Cause 2.

The edited ERR-8 needs ThreadShared at `?`. A raw pointer is not ThreadShared (THR-9 p11 64), and only Send may be vouched (TYP-43 p04 592-594: an unsafe extend of any interface but Send is E2040). So `rows = step(handle)?` is E2040 with no way through. Today ERR-8 p13 95 takes any `E: needs Error` and the program compiles. (`ref_to_ptr` is not imported; this is incidental.) Cause 3.

THR-15 (p11 336-337) makes `Sender` Send and ThreadShared and `Receiver` Send whatever their element, so a `shares Node` crosses with or without the edit. The edit touches neither THR-15 nor THR-2's routes (p11 99-106). This is the lead fix J7-07's gap.

IFC-4 (p05 417-419): inside the body `S.Failure` has only what its declared bounds give, `needs Error`. IFC-6 (p05 449-451): a `pub` function writes its bounds, and a missing one is E2040. The edited From bound needs Send and ThreadShared, so `text = src.read_all()?` is E2040 until `where S.Failure: needs (Send, ThreadShared)` is written. Today ERR-8 p13 95 accepts it. Cause 1.

Under the edited THR-8 (p11 51), `dyn Error` is Send only when Error requires it or the type names it. Error does neither (p13 87-88, p04 676), so `cause: owns dyn Error` makes ImportError neither Send nor ThreadShared, and its `?` into AnyError is E2040. The suggested `owns dyn Error + Send + ThreadShared` needs a dyn-to-dyn conversion for `source()`, and TYP-5's complete list (p04 71-86) has none. Today it compiles: Debug is implicit (STR-5 p05 239-241). The missing `from std.fmt import Formatter, FmtError` is incidental. Cause 1.

Same as S1-1, plus ERR-9 (p13 48-49), which still calls `-> Result[Texture]` "a function that can fail with any error". The edited ERR-8 refuses the parser's `?` while ERR-1 and ERR-9 accept it, so the assembled spec decides the program both ways. Without the edit all three agree. Cause 1.

The edit writes the spec's first `dyn I + Send`. THR-8 p11 53-54 and THR-9 p11 60-61 say the markers are written only in bounds. Verdict 109 (JOB.md 883-893) moved every list of needs after `needs`. decisions.md line 141 kept `+` after dyn as a lead's choice with no verdict, which OWNER-DIRECTION 226-229 counts among rules written without one. Beside an interface's `needs Send` (p11 51), this is a second spelling of one idea (checklist 11). Cause 2.

Same mechanism as S1-3. UploadError is vouched Send, but its `*u8` is not ThreadShared (THR-9 p11 64) and ThreadShared cannot be vouched (TYP-43 p04 592-594), so `n = upload(staging)?` is E2040 under the edit and compiles today. Cause 3.

With the edit an AnyError crosses threads. THR-2 (p11 119-121) runs the hand-over check on every object the handed value owns whose class has weakref links, one compare each, and for an erased error this goes through its table. The first answer's cost line, 'None', leaves it out. The language is right; the cost statement was wrong. Cause 4.

TYP-5 rule 8 (p04 84-86) converts to one interface, and the grammar's `dyn` bound list (p03 72, 171) is given a meaning by no rule, with or without the edit. `cmd: owns dyn Command + Send = owns Clear(color=3)` is undecided today in the same way. A gap for the list; the repaired edit does not depend on it.

causes.cause: The thread markers were put on the catch-all's conversion instead of on what an error is. So a bound `needs Error`, a field `owns dyn Error`, and the rules that say 'any error' (ERR-1, ERR-9) no longer carried what AnyError needs. Answered by ERR-3's property: Error requires Send and ThreadShared. Every `needs Error` (IFC-3: a bound brings its parents), every `dyn Error` (THR-8's existing clause) and AnyError then carry it, and ERR-1, ERR-8 and ERR-9 stay true as written.

The edit spelled a marker on an erased value as `dyn I + Send`, a second spelling of what an interface's `needs Send` already says, with no conversion rule behind it. Answered by withdrawing it: an erased value's markers come only from its interface's `needs` (THR-8's existing words, with ThreadShared as ODR-255 ruled), so no `+` and no new conversion are needed.

The catch-all needs ThreadShared, which no author may vouch for, so an error holding a raw pointer has no way in. This is not answered by this edit: it is group P04's pending ThreadShared vouch (J7-06), outside the allowed rules. It is stated as D's cost and presented with P04.

The cost line left out verdict 114's hand-over check, which reaches what an erased error owns through its table. Answered in the cost line: one indirect call per AnyError handed over, then one compare per owned object whose class has weakref links, and nothing where no class has them; to measure.

import std.thread
from std.sync import Sender, channel

interface Command:
    fn run() -> int
