existing_rule.rule: THR-8 (with ERR-8's description of what AnyError holds)
existing_rule.words: THR-8: "A type is **`Send`** when a value of it may be handed over to another thread: nothing reachable from it (its fields, its elements, what its `owns` parts hold, a function value's state) is a one-thread owner ... an `owns T` when `T` is; ... `dyn I` when `I` requires it (`interface I: needs Send:`)." ERR-8: "a `dyn Error` held alone (`owns dyn Error`) ... It implements `From[E]` for every `E: needs Error`". ERR-3: "`Error` is the interface of error types: `Display + Debug`" (no Send). THR-10: "`R` MUST be `Send` (`E7015`, `E7008`)". Together these decide today, with no one ever having chosen it, that AnyError is not Send, so the worker is refused at spawn. The compiler cannot tell what an erased error holds, so the only remaining choice is where to refuse. THR-8's property says a type-erased holder is safe for threads only when everything that may be put into it is. The choice is whether that is guaranteed where the value goes in or checked where it leaves the thread.

edits.before: a `dyn Error` held alone (`owns dyn Error`)
edits.after: an error that any thread may have and read, held alone (`owns dyn Error + Send + ThreadShared`)
edits.why_general: It states what the catch-all error holds as a property in its type: only errors any thread may have and read. THR-8's own derivation (an `owns T` is Send when `T` is; a dyn by what it may hold) then makes AnyError Send and ThreadShared on every route at once: a thread's result, a channel element, a job's data, a field of a thread_shared object, an RwLock, a `ref` given to scoped tasks. Nothing is added per route.

edits.before: It implements `From[E]` for every `E: needs Error`, so `?` converts any error into it,
edits.after: It is `Send` and `ThreadShared`, as everything it holds is (`[THR-8]`). It implements `From[E]` for every `E: needs (Error, Send, ThreadShared)`, so `?` converts any such error into it (`?` of one that is not both is `E2040`, whose message names the part that is not and the words to write, as `[THR-2]`'s does),
edits.why_general: The check sits where a value enters the erased holder, the one place the compiler still knows its type. So it covers every way in (`?`, `context`, `with_context`, `AnyError.from`, any generic use of `From`) and every kind of thing an error may hold: a shares owner, a weakref link, a sharedref mut link, a Cell, a thread-bound value. All of it comes from the marker rules, with no list of cases. It is the same shape as the owner's choice to refuse a thread_shared value where it is made (165).

edits.before: `dyn I` when `I` requires it (`interface I: needs Send:`).
edits.after: `dyn I` when every type it may hold is: when `I` requires it (`interface I: needs Send:`) or the type names it (`dyn I + Send`), and the same for `ThreadShared`.
edits.why_general: It states the property behind the old single case: a dyn value is safe for threads when everything that may be put into it is, whether its interface says so or its own type does. The `+` after `dyn` is already the grammar's (p03 line 72) and the lead kept it (decisions.md line 141). So the words also decide a program's own erased values (a renderer's command queue, a server's handlers) and ThreadShared as well as Send (THR-9 says it is inferred like Send). Nothing is added for AnyError.

answers.question: J6-16
answers.today: Refused at the `h = thread.spawn(...)` line, and the text never says so in words. `R` is `Result[int, AnyError]`, which must be Send (THR-10, p11 176). AnyError holds `owns dyn Error` (ERR-8, p13 94). `dyn Error` is Send only when Error requires Send (THR-8, p11 51), and Error requires only Debug and Display (ERR-3, p13 88; p04 676). The code is E7015 or E7008 (THR-10 names both). What the compiler does today is listed in to_verify. The danger the refusal guards against, in C++ terms: an exception object holding a non-atomic reference-counted pointer, rethrown on another thread through std::exception_ptr, so two threads race on the count.
answers.after: Compiles. It prints the file's length, or main returns the io error and prints `error: ...`. AnyError now holds only errors any thread may have and read, so it is Send, and the result crosses to the main thread. `io.Error` meets the new `From` bound at the `?` in `load`.
answers.decides: p13-errors.md 94-95 (ERR-8, new words: AnyError holds `owns dyn Error + Send + ThreadShared`, and `From[E]` is for `E: needs (Error, Send, ThreadShared)`), with p11-concurrency.md 51 (THR-8, new words: a dyn is Send when every type it may hold is) and 175-176 (THR-10: `R` MUST be Send).

sibling_cases.case: A server worker sends each request's Result over a channel (other construct: a channel instead of a thread's result; other software: a server).
sibling_cases.outcome: After: compiles and prints `/index`, then `error: empty request path`. `Result[String, AnyError]` is Send, so `Sender[Result[String]]` is too, and the thread's function may hold `tx`. Today: refused at the spawn line, because the function holds a Sender whose element is not Send (E7015).

sibling_cases.case: A game engine keeps load results, failures included, in an object shared by threads behind an RwLock (needs ThreadShared, not only Send; other software: a game engine's asset system).
sibling_cases.outcome: After: compiles and prints 1. `RwLock[Array[Result[Texture]]]` is ThreadShared because AnyError and Texture both are, so `thread_shared Assets()` passes the check at the line that makes it (verdict 165). Today: refused at `assets = thread_shared Assets()` (E7015), because AnyError is neither ThreadShared nor Send. It would also be refused under option E, where AnyError is Send only.

sibling_cases.case: A compiler's parser error holds a shared, one-thread owner of the source file and is passed into AnyError by `?`, in a program with one thread (the cost of the choice; other software: a compiler or parser).
sibling_cases.outcome: After: refused at `n = parse_header(file)?` with E2040. `ParseError.UnexpectedEnd` holds `file`, a `shares` owner that stays on one thread, so it cannot go into an AnyError. The message gives the words to write, as THR-2's does: hold a copy of what the error needs (`path: String` in place of `file: shares SourceFile`), or make the file `thread_shared` from the start. Naming `Result[int, ParseError]` on `compile` alone would not do, because main's `?` would hit the same check. Today: compiles and prints `error: unexpected end of input at byte 2`. This is the stated cost of option A: refused even with one thread, as Rust's anyhow refuses an `Rc` inside its error.

sibling_cases.case: A renderer's own erased command queue goes to another thread (other type: a program's own interface, not AnyError; other software: a renderer).
sibling_cases.program:
import std.thread
from std.sync import Sender, channel

interface Command:
    fn run() -> int

struct Clear:
    color: int

extend Clear implements Command:
    fn run() -> int:
        return this.color

fn record(tx: Sender[owns dyn Command + Send]):
    cmd: owns dyn Command + Send = owns Clear(color=3)
    tx.send(owns cmd).expect("renderer is gone")

fn main():
    tx, rx = channel[owns dyn Command + Send](capacity=16)
    recorder = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns tx: record(tx))
    total = 0
    for c in rx:
        total += c.run()
    recorder.join()
    println(total)
sibling_cases.outcome: After: compiles and prints 3. THR-8's new words make `dyn Command + Send` Send, because every type it may hold is, so the Sender may go to the recorder thread. A `Clear` holding a `shares mut` field would be refused at the line that turns it into `owns dyn Command + Send`. Today: THR-8's words cover only an interface that requires Send, so this element type is not said to be Send, and the spawn holding `tx` is refused (E7015) or left undecided.

readability.before:
import std.fs
import std.io
import std.thread

fn load(path: StrView) -> Result[int, io.Error]:   # a concrete error type, written only so the result may cross threads
    text = fs.read_to_string(path)?
    return Ok(text.len())

fn main() -> Result[void]:
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() => load("level1.cfg"))
    n = h.join()?                                   # io.Error -> AnyError here
    println(n)
    return Ok(())

# with a second kind of failure (a parse step), the worker also needs an @derive(Error) enum with an @from variant for each kind
readability.verdict: The after is shorter (no `import std.io`, no concrete error type) and reads like the one-thread program. With two kinds of failure it also saves a whole error enum. It adds no word. The cost falls only on the rare error that holds a one-thread owner, which is refused at its `?` with the words to write.

out.cost: None: decided when compiling. The `From` bound is checked at each `?` while compiling, and Send and ThreadShared are inferred. AnyError keeps its layout (the boxed error's data and table pointers, its identity, the context list) and its one allocation on the failure path (ERR-11), so a `?` into it costs what it costs today, and the success path costs nothing, as in C. To measure: confirm AnyError's size and the failure-path time are unchanged against today's build.

verdicts_kept.how: Untouched. An error holding a sharedref mut link is neither Send nor ThreadShared (164), so it cannot go into an AnyError, and no such link crosses threads inside one.

verdicts_kept.verdict: 23 (a shares value is never used from two threads)
verdicts_kept.how: Kept, and closed on one more route. An error holding a shares owner is refused at the `?` into AnyError, so an AnyError that crosses threads never carries one.

verdicts_kept.verdict: 61 (thread_shared fn(): the type says which threads may run it, chosen over the compiler finding it from the whole program)
verdicts_kept.how: Kept and followed. The catch-all error states in its type that any thread may have it (`dyn Error + Send + ThreadShared`), instead of a whole-program search (option C), which is the way 61 turned down.

verdicts_kept.verdict: 77 (reduction through two sharedref mut links from scoped tasks)
verdicts_kept.how: Untouched. Reductions and their checks do not change.

verdicts_kept.verdict: 93 (a task may take copy of t or ref t)
verdicts_kept.how: Kept. A `ref` to an AnyError may now go to a scoped task, because AnyError is ThreadShared. Otherwise the clash rule is unchanged.

verdicts_kept.verdict: 94 (thread.spawn takes a thread_shared fn())
verdicts_kept.how: Kept. spawn's signature and its rule that `R` must be Send are unchanged; AnyError now meets that rule.

verdicts_kept.verdict: 101 (two counts, the making thread deletes)
verdicts_kept.how: Untouched. A thread_shared object may now hold AnyError values, because they are Send and ThreadShared, and its counts work as before.

verdicts_kept.how: Untouched.

verdicts_kept.how: Kept. An AnyError holds no shares owner, so making or ending one in a scoped task touches no one-thread count.

decisions.title: Where an error that only one thread may have is refused: going into the catch-all error, or leaving the thread
decisions.problem: AnyError erases its error's type, so the compiler cannot tell whether a given AnyError holds an error with a one-thread owner. Today's rules, by accident and with no choice ever made, make AnyError unsafe to send. So an ordinary worker returning `Result[int]` is refused at `thread.spawn`, and the text never says so. Something must refuse the one-thread error somewhere. The choice is where.

options.code:
## std.core
pub struct AnyError:
    error: owns dyn Error + Send + ThreadShared
    ...
extend[E: needs (Error, Send, ThreadShared)] AnyError implements From[E]:
    ...
## user code unchanged
fn load(path: StrView) -> Result[int]:
    text = fs.read_to_string(path)?
    return Ok(text.len())
h = thread.spawn(owns fn() => load("level1.cfg"))
options.outcome: The worker compiles and prints the length. AnyError is Send and ThreadShared. `?` of an error that is not both (one holding a shares owner, a weakref link to a one-thread value, a sharedref mut link or a Cell) is refused at that `?` with E2040 and the words to write, even in a program with one thread. Rust's anyhow requires Send and Sync the same way.

Today's rules. The `Result[int]` worker is refused at the spawn line (E7015). A worker must name a concrete error type, which means an @derive(Error) enum with an @from variant per kind when it can fail two ways, and convert after join.

options.code:
## std unchanged; the compiler collects every error type converted into AnyError anywhere in the program
fn load(path: StrView) -> Result[int]:
    ...
h = thread.spawn(owns fn() => load("level1.cfg"))
options.outcome: The worker compiles until some `?` anywhere in the program, even in code that never meets a thread, puts a one-thread error into an AnyError. From then on every spawn, channel or thread_shared holder of AnyError is refused, with a message naming that distant line. It is the whole-program finding that verdict 61 turned down for function values.

The worker compiles. Every error type holding a one-thread owner is refused at its declaration (`@derive(Error)` or `implements Error`), even one that is never converted into AnyError and never leaves its thread.

options.code:
pub struct AnyError:
    error: owns dyn Error + Send
extend[E: needs (Error, Send)] AnyError implements From[E]:
options.outcome: The worker compiles. AnyError is Send but not ThreadShared, so `assets = thread_shared Assets()` holding `RwLock[Array[Result[Texture]]]` is refused at its line (verdict 165), and a `ref` to an AnyError cannot go to scoped tasks. Only an error holding a Cell-like part escapes refusal at `?`.

decisions.parameters_in_order: 1. The three goals at once: B fails 'Python-like', because the ordinary worker grows a concrete error type and an enum per kind; A, C, D and E keep it. 2. Safety (C4): every option refuses before a one-thread value crosses, so all are safe. 3. Compile time first (C5): all are decided when compiling and cost nothing at run time. 4. A written word only for meaning (C3): B forces an error type written only to satisfy a marker (bookkeeping); A, C, D and E write nothing. 5. Ordinary program no longer or harder (C2): E refuses an ordinary shared cache of load results; D refuses one-thread error types that never leave their thread, at their declaration; C lets an edit anywhere in the program break a spawn far away; A refuses only the `?` of a one-thread error into AnyError, which is rare and comes with the words to write. 6. Consistency (C6): A follows verdict 61 (the type says which threads may have it, not a whole-program search) and verdict 165 (refused where the value is made, not where it reaches a thread), ODR-255 (a dyn by what its interface requires), THR-2's message shape, and Rust's anyhow (Send + Sync). So A.
decisions.recommendation: A: the catch-all error may go to and be shared by any thread, and only errors that may are put into it. The rare error holding a one-thread owner is refused at its `?`, with the words to write.

owner_short.one_line: C++ analogue: can a catch-all exception holder (std::exception_ptr) cross threads, given it might hold an object with a non-atomic shared_ptr-like count?
owner_short.step_table:
| step | who | what happens | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | worker thread | `fs.read_to_string(path)?` puts the file error into the catch-all error | allowed: a file error may go to any thread |
| 2 | worker thread | returns `Result[int]` (count or catch-all error) from the thread | allowed: the catch-all holds only errors any thread may have |
| 3 | main thread | `n = h.join()?` | gets the count, or passes the error on |
| 4 | any code | `?` of an error holding a one-thread shared owner into the catch-all | refused when compiling at that line, with the line to write |
owner_short.today: The worker returning `Result[int]` is refused at `thread.spawn` without the text saying so; it must name a concrete error type instead.
options: A: the catch-all error is safe for every thread; an error that is not is refused where `?` puts it in, even in a one-thread program (as Rust's anyhow)
B: keep today: the catch-all stays on its thread; a worker names its own error type, an enum when it can fail two ways
C: the compiler searches the whole program; one one-thread error put in anywhere makes every thread hand-off of the catch-all fail, far from that line
D: every error type must be safe for every thread, refused where the error type is declared even if it never leaves its thread
E: the catch-all may be sent but not read by two threads at once; a shared cache of load results is refused
owner_short.recommendation: A: ordinary worker code compiles with nothing written, nothing costs anything at run time, and only the rare one-thread error is refused, at its own line with the fix.

to_verify: The compiler today on the J6-16 program: the spec says it is refused at the spawn line (E7015/E7008); check whether it is refused, or compiles because `R: Send` is not checked yet.

After std.core changes AnyError's field to `owns dyn Error + Send + ThreadShared` (core.em line 93) and the From extension to `[E: needs (Error, Send, ThreadShared)]` (core.em line 97): J6-16 compiles and prints the length.

The parser sibling: `n = parse_header(file)?` is E2040 at that line. The message names `file` (a shares owner), gives words that compile (`path: String` in place of `file: shares SourceFile`, or the file made thread_shared from the start), and does not suggest a concrete error type that main's `?` would then refuse.

`owns dyn I + Send` parses as a type, including as a generic argument (`channel[owns dyn Command + Send]`). It is inferred Send, and `+ ThreadShared` is inferred ThreadShared. Turning a type holding a shares or shares mut field into it is refused at that line.
`AnyError.source()` returns `Option[ref dyn Error]` from a held `dyn Error + Send + ThreadShared` (the marker bounds dropped) without error, and `downcast_ref` and `is` still work.

Every std error type that std or the examples pass into AnyError by `?` is Send and ThreadShared: io.Error, FmtError, Missing and Message (core.em), RangeError, and SendError[T] for the T's used. Every `?` into AnyError in std, the spec's examples and the test suites still compiles (regression scan).
ERR-10's `context` and `with_context` on `Result[T, E]` now need `E: Send + ThreadShared`, through `AnyError: From[E]`; check that the bound error is the E2040 named in ERR-8, not a different code.

The server sibling compiles and prints `/index` then `error: empty request path`. The game sibling compiles and prints 1, with `thread_shared Assets()` accepted. The renderer sibling compiles and prints 3.
Verdict 114's hand-over check reaches objects owned by the error inside an AnyError returned from a thread (through the dyn's table).
To measure: AnyError's size, and the time of a `?` into it on the failure path, are unchanged against today's build.
out.notes: ERR-1 (p13-errors.md 46-47) repeats the conversion bound in its list of what operations need of E: "converting one into `AnyError` takes any `E: needs Error`". It is outside the allowed rules, so it is not edited here. After this edit it must read `E: needs (Error, Send, ThreadShared)`, or the spec contradicts itself, so the lead has to align it. std/src/core.em lines 80-99 (the comment at 88 and the code at 93 and 97) must follow ERR-8. The `dyn I + Send` spelling is the grammar's (p03-grammar.md line 72, `bound_list` after `dyn`), kept by the lead's ruling in decisions.md line 141, and this would be the first time the spec writes it. If the owner later moves dyn to `needs`, these words follow that spelling. ThreadShared for a dyn is said in THR-8, because THR-9 is not an allowed rule; THR-9 says ThreadShared is inferred like Send, and ODR-255 already ruled that a dyn is Send/Sync by what its interface requires. Possible new gap, there before this edit and not changed by it: the spec does not say whether `owns dyn I`, and so AnyError, may hold an error that views a place (Rust's `'static` bound on anyhow). Per memory, an in-place edit to a cut hardening may only add text; this changes meaning, so the lead places it in a new hardening. Nothing was run. docs/AUTOPILOT.md and HANDOFF.md were skipped, as the workflow said review agents should. The relayed request to hibernate the laptop is for the orchestrator, not this step, so it was not acted on here.

checked: J6-16 program, line by line. Today it is refused at `h = thread.spawn(...)`: R is `Result[int, AnyError]`, which must be Send (THR-10 p11 175-176). AnyError holds `owns dyn Error` (p13 94; std/src/core.em 92-95). THR-8 p11 51 makes a `dyn I` Send only when `I` requires it, and `Error` requires only Debug and Display (p13 87-88; p04 676). So the code is E7015. With the edit it compiles: `fs.read_to_string(path)?` converts an io.Error, whose fields are kind, code and message: String (std/src/io.em 17-20), so it is Send and ThreadShared and meets the new From bound. AnyError's fields (`owns dyn Error + Send + ThreadShared`, u128, Array[String]) are all Send, so R is Send. Then `h.join()?` hands the error over unchanged (ERR-7 p13 82-83). Confirmed: it prints the length, or main returns the io error, which ERR-12 p13 109-112 prints as `error: ...` with exit 1.

Server sibling. The 'after' is confirmed (`/index`, then `error: empty request path`) once `AnyError.msg(owns ...)` is written. FN-2a p05 115-121 requires `owns` at the call for an owns parameter, and the program leaves it out. The spec's own ERR-8 example (p13 100-101) has the same slip, which predates this edit. The 'today' claim is refuted as the text stands: THR-15 p11 336-337 says `Sender` is Send and ThreadShared and `Receiver` is Send, whatever the element. A refusal at the spawn line rests on the lead fix J7-07, which is not in the text.

Game sibling. The 'after' is confirmed, printing 1. RwLock[T] is ThreadShared when T is Send and ThreadShared (THR-9 p11 66-67), and the class Texture is ThreadShared because its fields are (p04 578). So `thread_shared Assets()` passes THR-1 p11 82-85 and verdict 165. The 'today' refusal at that line is confirmed. The same missing `owns` in `AnyError.msg`.

Parser sibling. The 'after' is confirmed: E2040 at `n = parse_header(file)?`, because ERR-2 p13 51-52 routes `?` through `F.from` and the edited ERR-8 bounds that From. The 'today' is confirmed: it compiles, and main's Err prints `error: unexpected end of input at byte 2` on stderr (ERR-12). The derive holds because class objects implement Debug (p04 716). Naming `Result[int, ParseError]` on `compile` would not help, since main's `?` would hit the same check. Confirmed.

Renderer sibling. The 'after' is confirmed, printing 3, for a Clear that is Send. The edit also claims that a Clear holding a `shares mut` field is refused at the conversion line, but no rule says so (hole 2). The 'today' claim is refuted as the text stands, for the same THR-15 reason as the server sibling.

Cost. The bound is decided when compiling and AnyError's layout is unchanged, so that part of 'None' is right. But handing over an AnyError whose error owns a class object that weakref links point at now costs one call through the error's table (verdict 114 fix 1, reached through the dyn), on the failure path only. 'None' leaves this out. Not filed: it is the cost the owner accepted in verdict 114.
Verdicts 3, 23, 61, 77, 93, 94, 101, 104, 114, 164, 165 and 166 were checked against every program here. None is reversed or widened.

Views inside an AnyError. TYP-15 (p04 311-317) and LT-45 (p07 654-659) decide this by value: whatever holds a view, and every value holding that, lives no longer than what the view points into. So an AnyError holding a view of a local, stored where another thread may outlive the local, is E3063. The gap the edit's notes name (Rust's 'static) narrows to one thing to verify: how that tracking passes through a dyn conversion.

Hand-over through a dyn. THR-2 p11 112-122 covers 'every object the handed object owns whose class a weakref is made to', which includes the error inside an AnyError. How the check reaches through the dyn (a table entry) is not stated, the same as for any `interface I: needs Send` value today. To verify.

Effects through the dyn. An Error implementation that reads a static mut makes every unscoped thread that formats an AnyError refused (EFF-2's rule for dyn calls, with THR-20). That is the far-away break the decision held against option C, but it comes through verdict 86's accepted mechanism, and it is not a safety issue.

THR-8 edit, 'every type it may hold'. Read alone, this could mean a whole-program search (verdict 61 turned that down). The list after the colon (the interface requires it, or the type names it) makes it a property of the type. Not filed.

Two further programs found nothing new. First, a thread_shared ErrorLog holding `Mutex[Array[AnyError]]`, fed by workers: a Mutex is ThreadShared for a Send T (THR-9 p11 66). Second, an error holding `pool: thread_shared Pool` with Atomic fields: Send and ThreadShared when Pool is (THR-8 p11 50), and dropped on another thread by verdict 101's two counts.

The E2040 message for an error type from another package. Neither 'hold a copy' nor 'make it thread_shared from the start' can be written at the refused line. The fix that can be followed there is converting the error to text (`map_err` to `AnyError.msg`). This is message wording for the lead (checklist 9), so it is not filed as a hole.

matrix.guarantee: No data race on a one-thread count: no `shares` or `shares mut` owner, and no weakref link to a one-thread value, crosses threads inside an AnyError (C++: a non-atomic shared_ptr inside a std::exception_ptr rethrown on another thread).
matrix.how_kept: The edited ERR-8 (p13 94-95) makes AnyError hold `owns dyn Error + Send + ThreadShared`, with From only for `E: needs (Error, Send, ThreadShared)`. `?` goes through that From (ERR-2 p13 51-52), so an error holding such an owner or link is E2040 at its `?`. The edited THR-8 (p11 51) then makes AnyError Send. This is weakened by ERR-1 p13 46-47, which still states the old bound (hole 1).
matrix.must_refuse: parser_error_shares_owner_refused: E2040 at `n = parse_header(file)?`. err1_clash_shares_error_to_thread: E2040 at the same kind of line, before the spawn.
matrix.must_compile: anyerror_worker_result_crosses prints 10. j6_16_worker_loads_level compiles.

matrix.guarantee: No data race on shared reads: an AnyError that several threads read at once holds nothing a read may change (C++: a mutable cache inside a const object read by two threads).

class Mesh:
    name: String = String("")

@derive(Error)

outs.notes:
Engineering lens. The edit decides J6-16 and its four siblings as it claims. The broken flag comes from three medium holes, all caused by the edit, all in programs that compile today and have no threads.

1. Hole 1: generic error code (`[E: needs Error]`, or `type Failure: needs Error` on a library interface) that converts into AnyError must now write `Send, ThreadShared`.
2. Hole 2: an error with a boxed cause (`cause: owns dyn Error`) is refused. The fix's `source()` then needs a conversion that drops markers, which TYP-5's complete list (p04 71-86) does not give, so the message's line is not shown to compile.
3. Hole 3: ERR-1 (p13 46-47) and ERR-9 (p13 48-49) keep words the edit makes untrue, so the parser sibling is decided both ways.

Together these mean the decision's parameter walk, step 5, and the readability verdict ('adds no word'; 'the cost falls only on the rare error that holds a one-thread owner') do not state A's real costs.

Option D (the error interface requires Send and ThreadShared: an ERR-3 edit, plus this edit's 'the same for ThreadShared' in THR-8) avoids all three. Its own cost is that an error type holding a one-thread owner is refused where it is declared, even when it never enters AnyError. Under D the raw-pointer FFI error of hole 5 cannot implement Error at all, which is worse than under A. So A against D is a real trade-off for the owner, and the record should show both costs accurately. I make no ruling on it.

Low holes:
- the `+` spelling clashes with verdicts 109 and 61 and with THR-8/THR-9's 'written only in bounds';
- an FFI error vouched Send can never enter AnyError, since ThreadShared cannot be vouched (P04/J7-06);
- an unstated run-time cost: verdict 114's check goes through the dyn's table at each AnyError hand-over.

Pre-existing gaps, not holes of this edit:
- TYP-5 rule 8 names one interface, so `owns T` -> `owns dyn I + Send` is unstated (it was undecided before the edit too).
- THR-15 (p11 336) says a Sender is Send with no condition on its element. The server sibling's 'today: refused' rests on the lead's J7-07 fix, not on the text.
- THR-8's dyn clause says `dyn I`, which also names the parameter view. A view to another thread should need ThreadShared, as `ref T` does. The same issue exists today for `interface I: needs Send`.
- SendError implements no Error in the spec or std (sync.em 122), so `tx.send(v)?` into AnyError is undecided either way.
- The 'static/view question for `owns dyn Error` (noted by the edit) stands.

All error codes in the tests are the specification's (E2040, E7015), except T10, whose conversion code the specification does not name. Nothing was run: no compiler, no scripts. Files were only read. docs/AUTOPILOT.md and docs/HANDOFF.md were skipped, as the workflow says review agents should. The relayed request to hibernate the laptop is for the orchestrator after the workflow, not this step, so it was not acted on.

out.intent: Load a level file on a worker thread and hand back to the main thread either its length or the reason it failed.

existing_rule.words: THR-8: "A type is **`Send`** when a value of it may be handed over to another thread ... an `owns T` when `T` is; ... `dyn I` when `I` requires it (`interface I: needs Send:`)." ERR-3: "`Error` is the interface of error types: `Display + Debug` with `fn source() ...`" (p04 676: `interface Error: needs (Debug, Display):`, no Send). ERR-8: AnyError is "a `dyn Error` held alone (`owns dyn Error`)" implementing "`From[E]` for every `E: needs Error`". THR-10: "`R` MUST be `Send` (`E7015`, `E7008`)". IFC-3: "a bound brings its parents". Together they decide today, with no one having chosen it, that AnyError is not Send, so the worker is refused at spawn. The compiler cannot tell what an erased error holds; THR-8's own clause for a dyn already says how an erased value is made safe for threads: by what its interface requires. The choice is whether that requirement sits on what an error is, or on the catch-all's conversion.

edits.before: `Display + Debug` with `fn source() -> Option[ref dyn Error]` (default `None`) (§IV.8).
edits.after: `interface Error: needs (Debug, Display, Send, ThreadShared):` with `fn source() -> Option[ref dyn Error]` (default `None`) (§IV.8), so any thread may have and read every error, `dyn Error` and `AnyError` (`[THR-8]`). A type that is not `Send` and `ThreadShared` is `E2040` where it implements `Error`, the message naming what in it is not and the words to write (`[THR-2]`).
edits.why_general: It states the property on what an error is: any thread may have and read it. Every place that names an error then carries it with nothing written: a bound `E: needs Error` or `type Failure: needs Error` (a bound brings its parents, IFC-3 p05 411-413), a field `owns dyn Error`, and AnyError itself (THR-8's existing clause: a dyn is Send when its interface requires it). So every route is covered at once: a thread's result, a channel element, a job's data, a thread_shared holder, an RwLock, a `ref` given to a scoped task. The refusal sits where a type is made an error, the one place its contents are known, and the marker rules decide it for every one-thread part (a shares owner, a weakref link, a sharedref mut link, a Cell) with no list of cases. ERR-1's "any `E: needs Error`", ERR-8's `From` and ERR-9's "any error" stay true as written. The parents are spelled with `needs`, as verdict 110 spells them.

edits.before: `dyn I` when `I` requires it (`interface I: needs Send:`).
edits.after: `dyn I` when `I` requires it (`interface I: needs Send:`), as it is `ThreadShared` when `I` requires that (ODR-255).
edits.why_general: THR-9 says ThreadShared is inferred like Send but no rule says it for a dyn. ODR-255 already ruled that a dyn is Send and Sync (now ThreadShared) by what its interface requires. The words now say so for every interface, a program's own (`interface Command: needs (Send, ThreadShared):`) as well as Error. There is no second spelling: the markers go in the interface's `needs`, never after `dyn` with `+`.

answers.question: J6-16
answers.today: Refused at the `h = thread.spawn(...)` line, and the text never says so in words. `R` is `Result[int, AnyError]`, which must be Send (THR-10, p11 176). AnyError holds `owns dyn Error` (ERR-8, p13 94). `dyn Error` is Send only when Error requires Send (THR-8, p11 51), and Error requires only Debug and Display (ERR-3, p13 88; p04 676). The code is E7015 or E7008 (THR-10 names both). What the compiler does today is listed in to_verify. The danger the refusal guards against, in C++ terms: an exception object holding a non-atomic reference-counted pointer, rethrown on another thread through std::exception_ptr, so two threads race on the count.
answers.after: Compiles. It prints the file's length, or main returns the io error and prints `error: ...`. Error now requires Send and ThreadShared, so `dyn Error` is both (THR-8 p11 51), and so is AnyError, made of it, an identity and a list of Strings. The result crosses to the main thread. `io.Error` (a kind, a code, a String) is both, so it implements Error as before and its `?` into AnyError is unchanged.
answers.decides: p13-errors.md 88 (ERR-3, new words: `interface Error: needs (Debug, Display, Send, ThreadShared):`, and a type that is not both is E2040 where it implements Error), with p11-concurrency.md 51 (THR-8: a dyn is Send, and ThreadShared, when its interface requires it) and 175-176 (THR-10: `R` MUST be Send). ERR-8 (p13 93-95) is unchanged and now gives a Send and ThreadShared AnyError.

sibling_cases.case: A server worker sends each request's Result over a channel (other construct: a channel instead of a thread's result; other software: a server).
sibling_cases.outcome: After: compiles and prints `/index`, then `error: empty request path`. `Result[String, AnyError]` is Send, so the Sender may go to the worker under either reading of THR-15. Today: by THR-15's words (p11 336-337) a Sender is Send whatever its element, so the letter does not refuse it. That is the separate hole S1-4, which the lead fix J7-07 closes. With that fix it would be refused today, because AnyError is not Send.

sibling_cases.case: A game engine keeps load results, failures included, in an object shared by threads behind an RwLock (needs ThreadShared, not only Send; other software: a game engine's asset system).
sibling_cases.outcome: After: compiles and prints 1. `dyn Error` is ThreadShared because Error requires it (THR-8's new words), so AnyError is too. `RwLock[Array[Result[Texture]]]` is then ThreadShared (THR-9 p11 66-67), and `thread_shared Assets()` passes the check at the line that makes it (verdict 165). Today: refused at `assets = thread_shared Assets()` (E7015), because AnyError is neither Send nor ThreadShared. It would also be refused under option E, where AnyError is Send only.

sibling_cases.case: A parser library's generic entry point passes its source's error into AnyError (other construct: a generic function with an associated error type; other software: a library).
sibling_cases.outcome: After: compiles and prints 3, as today, with nothing added. `type Failure: needs Error` now brings Send and ThreadShared (IFC-3 p05 411-413: a bound brings its parents), so `S.Failure` meets AnyError's `From` (ERR-8 p13 95). Under option A this line was E2040 until `where S.Failure: needs (Send, ThreadShared)` was written (hole E1-1).

sibling_cases.case: An asset importer's error wraps the reader's own failure in an `owns dyn Error` field (other type: an erased error inside an error; other software: an asset pipeline).
sibling_cases.outcome: After: compiles as today. It prints the length, or `error: cannot import hero.mesh` then `caused by: <io message>` (ERR-12 p13 109-112). `owns dyn Error` is Send and ThreadShared because Error requires both (THR-8 p11 51), so ImportError is both and implements Error. `source()` returns the same type it holds, so no conversion is needed. Under option A it was E2040 at `n = import_mesh(...)?`, and the suggested `owns dyn Error + Send + ThreadShared` needed a conversion the spec does not have (hole E1-2).

sibling_cases.case: A compiler's parser error holds a shared, one-thread owner of the source file, in a program with one thread (the cost of the choice; other software: a compiler or parser).
sibling_cases.outcome: After: refused at `@derive(Error)` on `ParseError` with E2040. `UnexpectedEnd` holds `file`, a `shares` owner that stays on one thread, and an error may go to any thread. The message gives the words to write, as THR-2's does: hold a copy of what the error needs (`path: String` in place of `file: shares SourceFile`, built with `path=copy of file.path`), or make the file `thread_shared` from the start. Today: compiles and prints `error: unexpected end of input at byte 2`. This is option D's stated cost: refused at the error type's own line even with one thread, and even where it never goes into AnyError. Under A the same error was refused at its `?`, which nearly every error reaches because main returns AnyError.

readability.before:
import std.fs
import std.io
import std.thread

fn load(path: StrView) -> Result[int, io.Error]:   # a concrete error type, written only so the result may cross threads
    text = fs.read_to_string(path)?
    return Ok(text.len())

fn main() -> Result[void]:
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() => load("level1.cfg"))
    n = h.join()?                                   # io.Error -> AnyError here
    println(n)
    return Ok(())

# with a second kind of failure (a parse step), the worker also needs an @derive(Error) enum with an @from variant for each kind
readability.verdict: The after is shorter (no `import std.io`, no concrete error type) and reads like the one-thread program. With two kinds of failure it also saves a whole error enum. It adds no word anywhere. Generic error code (`type Failure: needs Error`) and error wrappers holding `owns dyn Error` stay exactly as today, where option A made them grow `needs (Send, ThreadShared)` and `+ Send + ThreadShared`. The cost falls only on an error type holding a one-thread part, which is refused at its own declaration with the words to write.

out.cost: Compile time: Send and ThreadShared are inferred, and are checked once, where a type implements Error. A `?` into AnyError is checked as today. Run time: AnyError keeps its layout (the boxed error's data and table pointers, its identity, the context list) and its one allocation on the failure path (ERR-11). A `?` into it costs what it costs today, and the success path costs nothing, as in C. Handing an AnyError to another thread runs verdict 114's hand-over check on what its error owns (THR-2 p11 119-121) through the error's table: one indirect call per AnyError handed over, then one compare for each object it owns whose class has weakref links. Nothing runs in a program where no class has weakref links. C pays nothing to pass an error pointer to another thread. To measure: AnyError's size and failure-path time against today's build, and the time of that hand-over check.

decisions.title: Where an error that only one thread may have is refused: where its type is declared an error, where it goes into the catch-all error, or where it leaves the thread
decisions.problem: AnyError erases its error's type, so the compiler cannot tell whether a given AnyError holds an error with a one-thread part. Today's rules make AnyError unsafe to send, by accident and with no choice ever made. So an ordinary worker returning `Result[int]` is refused at `thread.spawn`, and the text never says so. Something must refuse the one-thread error somewhere. The first answer put the check on the catch-all's conversion (A). The breakers showed that A also makes ordinary generic error code and error wrappers write thread words, makes the rules that say 'any error' untrue, and needs a new `dyn I + Send` spelling with no conversion rule behind it.

options.code:
## std.core
pub struct AnyError:
    error: owns dyn Error + Send + ThreadShared
    ...
extend[E: needs (Error, Send, ThreadShared)] AnyError implements From[E]:
    ...
## a generic library
[S: needs Source]
pub fn count_lines(src: S) -> Result[int] where S.Failure: needs (Send, ThreadShared):
    text = src.read_all()?
## an error wrapper
struct ImportError:
    cause: owns dyn Error + Send + ThreadShared
options.outcome: The worker compiles. A one-thread error is refused at its `?` into AnyError (E2040), even with one thread. Generic code whose error is only `needs Error` must also write `where S.Failure: needs (Send, ThreadShared)`. A wrapper holding `owns dyn Error` must write `owns dyn Error + Send + ThreadShared`, which is a second spelling of the markers, and its `source()` then needs a conversion the spec does not have. ERR-1's 'any `E: needs Error`' and ERR-9's 'any error' become untrue.

Today's rules. The `Result[int]` worker is refused at the spawn line (E7015). A worker must name a concrete error type: an @derive(Error) enum with an @from variant per kind when it can fail two ways, converted after join.

options.code:

fn load(path: StrView) -> Result[int]:
    ...
h = thread.spawn(owns fn() => load("level1.cfg"))
options.outcome: The worker compiles until some `?` anywhere in the program, even in code that never meets a thread, puts a one-thread error into an AnyError. From then on every spawn, channel or thread_shared holder of AnyError is refused, with a message naming that distant line. This is the whole-program search that verdict 61 turned down for function values.

The worker compiles. Generic error code (`needs Error`) and wrappers holding `owns dyn Error` compile with nothing written, and every rule that says 'any error' stays true. An error type holding a one-thread part (a shares owner, a weakref link to a one-thread value, a sharedref mut link, a Cell) is refused where it implements Error (E2040, with the words to write), even if it never leaves its thread. One holding a raw pointer is refused until its author may vouch for ThreadShared, which is the pending vouching question (P04, J7-06); A refused the same error at its `?`. This is Swift's choice: its Error refines Sendable.

options.code:
pub struct AnyError:
    error: owns dyn Error + Send
extend[E: needs (Error, Send)] AnyError implements From[E]:
options.outcome: The worker compiles. AnyError is Send but not ThreadShared, so `assets = thread_shared Assets()` holding `RwLock[Array[Result[Texture]]]` is refused at its line (verdict 165), and a `ref` to an AnyError cannot go to scoped tasks. It has A's costs for Send: generic bounds and dyn fields must name it.

decisions.parameters_in_order: 1. The three goals at once. B fails 'Python-like', because the ordinary worker grows a concrete error type and an enum per kind. A and E fail it for ordinary library and error-wrapping code, which grows thread words (holes E1-1, E1-2). C and D keep all of it as today. 2. Safety (C4): every option refuses before a one-thread value crosses. A's safety for program-defined erased types also rested on a conversion to `dyn I + Send` that no rule states (hole S1-2); D needs no such conversion. 3. Compile time first (C5): all are decided when compiling. Each adds only verdict 114's existing hand-over check, through a table, when an AnyError crosses (stated in cost). 4. A written word only for meaning (C3): A writes `needs (Send, ThreadShared)` in generic bounds and `+ Send + ThreadShared` on dyn fields, words that say nothing the program does (bookkeeping). B writes a concrete error type. C and D write nothing. 5. Ordinary program no longer or harder (C2): C lets an edit anywhere break a spawn far away. D refuses only an error type holding a one-thread part, at its own line with the words to write. These are the same errors A refused at their `?`, which nearly every error reaches since main returns AnyError, plus the rare one that never leaves its thread. 6. Consistency (C6): D uses THR-8's existing clause (a dyn is Send by what its interface requires) and ODR-255, IFC-3 (a bound brings its parents), verdict 110's `needs` spelling, verdict 61 (the type says which threads may have it), verdict 165 (refused where it is made), no `+` (verdict 109; decisions.md line 141 left `+` after dyn unanswered), and Swift's Error: Sendable. It keeps ERR-1, ERR-8 and ERR-9 true as written. So D.
decisions.departs_from_verdict: none. Verdict 110 settled how Error's parents are spelled (`needs (Debug, Display)`); this keeps that spelling and adds two parents to the list, which no verdict decided.
decisions.recommendation: D: every error type may go to and be read by any thread, checked where the type is declared an error. The catch-all error, generic error code and error wrappers then need no word, and only an error type holding a one-thread part is refused, at its own line with the words to write. Present it with the pending ThreadShared vouch (P04, J7-06), which decides the raw-pointer error.

owner_short.one_line: C++ analogue: should every exception type be required to be safe to hand to and read from any thread, so that a catch-all holder like std::exception_ptr can always cross threads?
owner_short.step_table:
| step | who | what happens | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | an error type's author | declares an error holding plain values (a code, a text) | allowed: it may go to any thread |
| 2 | worker thread | `fs.read_to_string(path)?` puts the file error into the catch-all error | allowed, nothing written |
| 3 | worker thread | returns `Result[int]` (count or catch-all error) from the thread | allowed: every error may go to any thread |
| 4 | main thread | `n = h.join()?` | gets the count, or passes the error on |
| 5 | an error type's author | declares an error holding a one-thread shared owner | refused when compiling at that declaration, with the line to write |
owner_short.today: The worker returning `Result[int]` is refused at `thread.spawn` without the text saying so; it must name a concrete error type instead.
options: A: the catch-all error is safe for every thread and checks each error where `?` puts it in; generic error code and error wrappers must then add thread words
B: keep today: the catch-all stays on its thread; a worker names its own error type, an enum when it can fail two ways
C: the compiler searches the whole program; one one-thread error put in anywhere makes every thread hand-off of the catch-all fail, far from that line
D: every error type is safe for every thread (as Swift's errors are), checked where the error type is declared; nothing is written anywhere else
E: the catch-all may be sent but not read by two threads at once; a shared cache of load results is refused
owner_short.recommendation: D: ordinary worker, library and error-wrapping code compile with nothing written; only an error type holding a one-thread part is refused, at its own declaration with the fix (one holding a raw pointer waits on the pending question of vouching for thread sharing).

The spec then decides `n = parse_header(file)?` both ways. ERR-2 (p13 51-52) routes `?` through `F.from`, so the race needs ERR-1's reading, but the contradiction is the edit's: without it the two rules agree. Cause 1.

TYP-5 rule 8 (p04 84-86) converts only to "an interface its type implements", and no rule or code refuses that line. Today THR-8 does not make that type Send, so the spawn is refused whatever the conversion does. Cause 2.

The edited ERR-8 needs ThreadShared at `?`. A raw pointer is not ThreadShared (THR-9 p11 64), and only Send may be vouched (TYP-43 p04 592-594: an unsafe extend of any interface but Send is E2040). So `rows = step(handle)?` is E2040 with no way through. Today ERR-8 p13 95 takes any `E: needs Error` and the program compiles. (`ref_to_ptr` is not imported; this is incidental.) Cause 3.

THR-15 (p11 336-337) makes `Sender` Send and ThreadShared and `Receiver` Send whatever their element, so a `shares Node` crosses with or without the edit. The edit touches neither THR-15 nor THR-2's routes (p11 99-106). This is the lead fix J7-07's gap.

Under the edited THR-8 (p11 51), `dyn Error` is Send only when Error requires it or the type names it. Error does neither (p13 87-88, p04 676), so `cause: owns dyn Error` makes ImportError neither Send nor ThreadShared, and its `?` into AnyError is E2040. The suggested `owns dyn Error + Send + ThreadShared` needs a dyn-to-dyn conversion for `source()`, and TYP-5's complete list (p04 71-86) has none. Today it compiles: Debug is implicit (STR-5 p05 239-241). The missing `from std.fmt import Formatter, FmtError` is incidental. Cause 1.

Same as S1-1, plus ERR-9 (p13 48-49), which still calls `-> Result[Texture]` "a function that can fail with any error". The edited ERR-8 refuses the parser's `?` while ERR-1 and ERR-9 accept it, so the assembled spec decides the program both ways. Without the edit all three agree. Cause 1.

The edit writes the spec's first `dyn I + Send`. THR-8 p11 53-54 and THR-9 p11 60-61 say the markers are written only in bounds. Verdict 109 (JOB.md 883-893) moved every list of needs after `needs`. decisions.md line 141 kept `+` after dyn as a lead's choice with no verdict, which OWNER-DIRECTION 226-229 counts among rules written without one. Beside an interface's `needs Send` (p11 51), this is a second spelling of one idea (checklist 11). Cause 2.

With the edit an AnyError crosses threads. THR-2 (p11 119-121) runs the hand-over check on every object the handed value owns whose class has weakref links, one compare each, and for an erased error this goes through its table. The first answer's cost line, 'None', leaves it out. The language is right; the cost statement was wrong. Cause 4.

TYP-5 rule 8 (p04 84-86) converts to one interface, and the grammar's `dyn` bound list (p03 72, 171) is given a meaning by no rule, with or without the edit. `cmd: owns dyn Command + Send = owns Clear(color=3)` is undecided today in the same way. A gap for the list; the repaired edit does not depend on it.

causes.cause: The thread markers were put on the catch-all's conversion instead of on what an error is. So a bound `needs Error`, a field `owns dyn Error`, and the rules that say 'any error' (ERR-1, ERR-9) no longer carried what AnyError needs. Answered by ERR-3's property: Error requires Send and ThreadShared. Every `needs Error` (IFC-3: a bound brings its parents), every `dyn Error` (THR-8's existing clause) and AnyError then carry it, and ERR-1, ERR-8 and ERR-9 stay true as written.

The edit spelled a marker on an erased value as `dyn I + Send`, a second spelling of what an interface's `needs Send` already says, with no conversion rule behind it. Answered by withdrawing it: an erased value's markers come only from its interface's `needs` (THR-8's existing words, with ThreadShared as ODR-255 ruled), so no `+` and no new conversion are needed.

The catch-all needs ThreadShared, which no author may vouch for, so an error holding a raw pointer has no way in. This is not answered by this edit: it is group P04's pending ThreadShared vouch (J7-06), outside the allowed rules. It is stated as D's cost and presented with P04.

The cost line left out verdict 114's hand-over check, which reaches what an erased error owns through its table. Answered in the cost line: one indirect call per AnyError handed over, then one compare per owned object whose class has weakref links, and nothing where no class has them; to measure.

holes.program:
import std.thread
from std.sync import RwLock

class Texture:
    width: int = 0

class Assets:                              # a game engine's asset cache, shared by its loader threads
    loaded: RwLock[Array[Texture]] = RwLock([])

fn unload_all(assets: thread_shared Assets):
    with g = assets.loaded.write():
        g.clear()                          # ends every Texture, on this thread

fn main():
    assets = thread_shared Assets()
    hero = Texture(width=64)
    preview = weakref hero                 # a one-thread link: hero's weak count is plain
    with g = assets.loaded.write():
        g.push(owns hero)                  # hero is now reachable from every thread
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() thread_shared assets: unload_all(assets))
    if preview exists as p:
        println(p.width)
    else:
        println("gone")
    h.join()

RC-4 point 4 (p08 173-178) lists 'into a lock-guarded thread_shared container' as a place other threads reach, but only for owners of thread_shared values. No rule says that `g.push(owns hero)` moves hero away from `preview`.

holes.what_goes_wrong: If the store is not a hand-over, the worker's `g.clear()` ends hero and marks its header with plain writes while main's `preview exists as p` tests that header and reads `p.width`. That is a data race on a one-thread weak count and a read of an ended object (C++: a weak_ptr::lock racing the last shared_ptr's release on a non-atomic control block). If it is a hand-over, main prints `gone`. The words do not decide which.
holes.fix_hint: An object stored where another thread can reach it is handed over at that store, for its one-thread links as for its counts, at every place RC-4 point 4 lists.

import std.thread
from std.fmt import Formatter, FmtError

class SaveSlot:
    index: int = 0

open class GameError:                      # a game's base error type
    message: String

    fn init(owns message: String):
        this.message = message

extend GameError implements Display:
    fn fmt(ref mut f: Formatter) -> Result[void, FmtError]:
        return f.write_str(this.message)

extend GameError implements Error:
    pass

class SaveError(GameError):                # the save system's error, keeping the slot it failed on
    slot: shares SaveSlot

    fn init(owns message: String, slot: shares SaveSlot):
        this.slot = shares slot
        super.init(owns message)

fn save(slot: shares SaveSlot) -> Result[int, GameError]:
    return Err(SaveError(owns String("disk full"), shares slot))   # upcast to GameError

fn main():
    slot = shares SaveSlot()
    r = save(slot)
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns r: r.is_err())
    again = shares slot
    println(h.join(), again.index)
holes.today: Compiles. Class objects are Send when every component is (THR-8 p11 47-48), and GameError's only field is a String, so R = Result[int, GameError] is Send (THR-10 p11 176). TYP-5 rule 8 (p04 86) upcasts the SaveError, and no rule says a derived class must keep its base's markers (CLS-4 p05 335-345 says nothing of them).
holes.with_edit: The same for this program. The AnyError route (save returning `Result[int]`, with `?`) depends on whether a class that gets Error through its base 'implements Error' under ERR-3's new E2040. The edit's words do not say.
holes.what_goes_wrong: The worker ends `r`, so the SaveError and its `slot` owner, with a plain subtract while main's `again = shares slot` adds. The count is lost and the slot is later read after it is freed (C++: a derived exception holding a non-atomic shared_ptr, caught by base reference on another thread).

tests.program:
import std.thread
from std.sync import Receiver, channel

class Node:
    hits: int = 0

fn count(rx: Receiver[shares Node]) -> int:
    n = 0
    for node in rx:
        n += node.hits
    return n

fn main():
    tx, rx = channel[shares Node](capacity=4)
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns rx: count(rx))
    root = shares Node()
    tx.send(owns shares root).expect("counter is gone")
    keep = shares root
    println(keep.hits)

holes.with_edit: Three refusals, one after another. (1) `extend[T] PoolFull[T] implements Error:` is E2040. A struct is Send and ThreadShared only when its fields are (THR-8 p11 48, THR-9 p11 63), so `PoolFull[T]` is both only for a T that is. Implementers of an interface implement its parents (IFC-3 p05 411), and inside a generic T has only its declared bounds (IFC-4 p05 417-418). The new ERR-3 words refuse a type that is not both 'where it implements Error'. The words to write are `extend[T: needs (Send, ThreadShared)] PoolFull[T] implements Error:`. (2) With those words, `pool.insert(owns x)?` in `pub fn fill` is E2040. `PoolFull[T]` is an Error only for such a T, and a pub function writes its bounds (IFC-6 p05 449-453), so it needs `[T: needs (Send, ThreadShared)]` above `pub fn fill`. (3) Then main's `fill(ref mut pool, owns wave)` is E2040: `shares Enemy` is not Send (THR-8 p11 45), in a program with one thread. Under the other reading (Error implemented only for the instances that meet the markers, which no rule states for an interface's parents), step 1 passes and steps 2 and 3 stand.
holes.what_goes_wrong: A common kind of generic library error hands the caller's value back. Rust has `SendError<T>`, `TrySendError<T>` and arrayvec's `CapacityError<T>`; std's own SendError[T] holds the value it could not send. Under the edit such an error needs thread words where it implements Error, and again in every pub generic function that uses `?` on it. The one-thread game whose pool holds `shares` owners is refused at its call, far from any error declaration. These are A's costs: E1-1's bound, and the refusal at the use rather than at the declaration. The edit says D removes them. Its readability verdict says 'It adds no word anywhere'. Decision parameter 4 says 'C and D write nothing'. why_general says 'every place that names an error then carries it with nothing written'. The cost section says the refusal is 'at its own declaration ... the one place its contents are known', but a generic error's contents are not known there. Under A this library's extend line needed nothing, so here D writes more words than A, not fewer. The owner would compare A and D on a wrong account.

outs.notes:
Engineering lens, specification only: nothing was run. Following the workflow, I skipped docs/AUTOPILOT.md and docs/HANDOFF.md, which are for compiler work. The relayed request to hibernate the laptop belongs to the orchestrator after the workflow ends; I did not act on it in this step.

Result: the repaired edit (option D) removes the first round's causes 1, 2 and 4. Generic code bounded by `needs Error`, wrappers holding `owns dyn Error`, and ERR-1, ERR-8 and ERR-9 all hold as written. The question's program and the five siblings behave as the edit states, with two exceptions: the cross-rule clash (hole 3), and two small spelling slips listed below.

Three medium holes caused by the edit, so broken is true:
- Hole 1. A generic error that hands the caller's value back (`PoolFull[T]`) needs `[T: needs (Send, ThreadShared)]` where it implements Error and again in every pub generic function that uses `?` on it. A one-thread instance is then refused at its use. These are A's costs, and the decision record says D removes them ('It adds no word anywhere'; 'C and D write nothing').
- Hole 2. `@derive(Error)` on a generic type is left undecided; the edit's own to_verify says 'decide which'. Under the per-instance reading, a one-thread program silently loses its `caused by:` line (ERR-12).
- Hole 3. ERR-3 now declares Error's parents differently from the definitions in IV.8 that it cites (p04 600-601, 676: 'These are the definitions'). So J6-16 and every sibling are decided both ways. This is the same kind of clash as S1-1 and E1-3; the repair moved it rather than removing it.

Holes 1 and 2 share one cause: Error's marker parents make whether a generic type is an error depend on its payload, and neither the words nor the cost line say how.

One low hole: an erased `owns dyn Display` field (or a plain `fn()` field). The words THR-2 offers do not compile for it, and the edit's cost list leaves it out.

First-round holes:
- S1-4 and E1-7, re-tested: still pre_existing.
- S1-3 and E1-5 (raw pointer; ThreadShared cannot be vouched for): still stand under D, now refused at the `implements Error` line. They are low, acknowledged by the repair and deferred to P04 (J7-06), so I did not file them again.

Accuracy slips in the answer:
- The importer sibling lacks `owns` before the lambda given to `map_err` (verdict 158). The server sibling's `AnyError.msg(f"...")` lacks `owns` (verdict 147), but the spec's own ERR-8 example (p13 100-101) has the same slip, so that one is pre-existing. The tests above use the corrected spelling.
- to_verify lists SendError[T] and FmtError as Error implementers, but neither std (sync.em 121-126, fmt.em 21-22) nor the spec implements Error for them.

Wording, not holes:
- ERR-3's 'a type that is not Send and ThreadShared' reads more clearly as 'not both Send and ThreadShared'.
- THR-8's 'as it is ThreadShared when I requires that' can be read as giving a reason; 'and is ThreadShared when I requires that' would avoid it.

Possible further gap, already there before this edit and named in the edit's notes: an error that holds a view (TYP-34) inside AnyError now counts as Send, and the spec does not say whether erasing the error into AnyError keeps the view's limit on how long it may live.

verdicts.evidence: Today the program compiles. Error's parents are only Debug and Display (p13 87-88; p04 676), and the program writes both for every T, so `extend[T] PoolFull[T] implements Error` holds for every T. AnyError's `From[E]` takes every `E: needs Error` (p13 95), so `[T]` is all `pub fn fill` needs. With the edit, ERR-3 makes Send and ThreadShared parents of Error, and implementers must implement their parents (IFC-3 p05 411). A struct is Send or ThreadShared only when every field is (THR-8 p11 48; THR-9 p11 63), and inside a generic body T has only what its bounds give (TYP-17 p04 461-462). So `PoolFull[T]` for an unbounded T is not Send, and the edit's own words, 'E2040 where it implements Error', refuse the extend line. The fix, `extend[T: needs (Send, ThreadShared)]`, makes `PoolFull[T]` an Error only for such a T. Then `pool.insert(owns x)?` in `pub fn fill` needs a bound the function does not write, which is E2040 (TYP-17 p04 462-466; IFC-6 p05 449-453). After that, main's call with `shares Enemy`, which is not Send (THR-8 p11 45), is refused in a program with one thread. Under the per-instance reading the extend passes, but the fill and main steps still stand. The edit says 'It adds no word anywhere', 'C and D write nothing', and that the refusal is 'at its own declaration'. For a generic error type that holds a T, all three are untrue: the bounds are written in the extend and in every pub generic function, and the refusal comes at a use far away. The behaviour changes against today, and the cost statement the owner would compare is wrong, the same kind as E1-6. (`rejected=v` may need `owns v`; this is incidental.)

Today: `shares Asset` has Debug, because a class handle always has Debug (TYP-36 table p04 716; ODR-113). io.Error is an Error. So `@derive(Error)` gives `LoadError[shares Asset]` Display, Debug and Error (p13 89-92), and main's Err prints `error: ...` and then `caused by: ...` (ERR-12 p13 109-111). With the edit, `LoadError[T]` is Send and ThreadShared only for some T (THR-8 p11 45, 48), and the edited ERR-3 says only 'E2040 where it implements Error'. It does not say whether a generic derive implements Error for each instance or is refused. The edit's own to_verify says 'decide which'. Reading (i), per instance as STR-5's implicit derives work (p05 239-241): `LoadError[shares Asset]` is not an Error. Its `@from` From is still given (p13 91-92), main needs only `E: needs Display` (FN-8 p05 189-190), and ERR-12's last sentence applies: 'Display but not Error has no chain and prints its message alone' (p13 111-112). The `caused by:` line is dropped without any message. Reading (ii): E2040 at the derive. The only bound the enum can take, `T: needs (Send, ThreadShared)`, then refuses `LoadError[shares Asset]` in load_list's signature. Without the edit, this program prints its chain under either reading: the per-instance question exists today only for a T without Debug, which `shares Asset` is not. So the program goes wrong only because of the edit, and the edit leaves which way it goes undecided.

The edited ERR-3 (p13 87-88) declares `interface Error: needs (Debug, Display, Send, ThreadShared):` and cites §IV.8. §IV.8 introduces its block with 'These are the definitions; `std.core` declares them' (p04 600-601), and that block still reads `interface Error: needs (Debug, Display):` (p04 676). TYP-17's example repeats it (p04 459), and so does std/src/core.em line 80. The block is not marked Note or Example, which are the only non-normative texts (p00 102-103), and the specification has no rule saying which of two normative texts wins. THR-8 makes `dyn Error` Send only 'when I requires it' (p11 51), so J6-16's `R` (THR-10 p11 176) is Send under ERR-3 and not Send under IV.8. The assembled specification decides the program both ways. Today ERR-3 ('Display + Debug', p13 88) and p04 676 agree, so the edit creates the disagreement. Its own notes confirm it: 'until the lead writes it the sketch disagrees with ERR-3'. The first round counted the same kind of disagreement as real (S1-1, E1-3).

out.notes: I checked all three holes against the part files, plus std/src/core.em line 80 and std/src/sync.em lines 117-126. Nothing was run, and I skipped docs/AUTOPILOT.md and docs/HANDOFF.md, as the workflow says review agents should. E2-2: the 'today' column relies on `shares Asset` having Debug, which TYP-36 (p04 716) and ODR-113 support for class handles. Severities are left as the breakers gave them.
