final.intent: Build a C++ renderer with its (width, height) constructor, then draw a mesh and a sprite through its two `draw` overloads, running the functions the C++ header means.

existing_rule.words: `super.init(…)` selects the C++ base constructor by arity and argument types and runs it at `super.init(…)` (`[CLS-11]`)

edits.before: There is no overloading: two functions of one name in one scope are `E1030`, except operator-interface implementations and `extend` blocks for different types.
edits.after: A C++ name of several functions imports as one name (`[FFI-39b]`): the header, not the program, declares them.
edits.why_general: Says why the no-overloading rule does not reach a header (principle 6). Refusing a header's overloads would refuse correct programs over code they did not write and cannot change. It covers every C++ name of several functions (namespace functions, methods, static functions, constructors) without naming any of them.

edits.before: `super.init(…)` selects the C++ base constructor by arity and argument types and runs it at `super.init(…)` (`[CLS-11]`); a base with no default constructor and no declared `init` is `E5058`.
edits.after: Each use of a C++ name of several functions (as `[FFI-30]` counts them) stands for the one it fits, ranked as `[TYP-24]` ranks instances, an untyped literal counting as C++ types it (`c_int`, `f64`) and an object as `ref` through a name that only reads it or in an entry with `@ffi(const)`, else `ref mut`: a call (`new`, `super.init(…)`) by its object and its arguments' number, names, types and words; an `override fn` by its parameters; a function value by its expected callable type; an overlay entry by what it writes. What the code around it permits is checked after, on the one chosen. None, or several fitting equally, is `E2070` (an entry `E5010`), naming each.
edits.why_general: One property for every use of such a name, not just calls. A use stands for the one function it fits, ranked the way Ember already ranks an interface's instances (exact type before coercion). Literals count as C++ types them, and the object counts as C++ counts its implied object, so where C++ picks a function Ember picks the same one or refuses. Nothing more is needed for constructors, `super.init`, methods, namespace functions, overrides, function values and overlay entries. A redeclared function counts once. What the code around a use permits (unsafe code, effects, values handed over, threads, views) is checked on the chosen function, so a line runs the same function wherever it stands. A use that fits nothing, or ties, is refused with the candidates named.

edits.before: In an entry marked `@ffi(macro_fn)` (`[FFI-6b]`) a parameter's and the result's words are one Ember type each (`IDENT ":" type`, `"->" type`), since a macro has no C declaration to read (ODR-147).
edits.after: An entry may write each parameter's and the result's word and type as imported (`owns value: Texture`), checked, before its contract words; `[FFI-30c]` and `[FFI-55]` count entries by function.
edits.why_general: The single entry form gets an optional typed parameter. It is Ember's own spelling of a parameter, already written in `@ffi(macro_fn)` entries. With FFI-39b's 'an overlay entry by what it writes', the type is needed exactly where parameter names cannot tell functions apart; elsewhere it may be written and is checked. Every overlay rule that counts entries (`override`, a second entry, the `ember.overlays` record) then counts per function, for every overloaded name.

answers.question: J8-04
answers.today: Undecided, and refused if read literally. FFI-39b (p21-annex-c.md 128-129) picks a C++ constructor by arity and argument types only for `super.init`. Nothing says which `new` or `draw` a call runs. TYP-26 (p04-types.md 867-868) reads `Renderer`'s two `new` and two `draw` as 'two functions of one name in one scope', which is `E1030`. In the overlay, FFI-12 tells the two `draw` entries apart by their parameter names, but FFI-30c (p16-ffi.md 221-222) makes 'any other second entry for one name' `E5010`.
answers.after: Compiles. `Renderer.new(1280, 720)` runs `Renderer(int, int)`, the only constructor that takes two arguments. `r.draw(mesh)` runs `draw(const Mesh&)` and `r.draw(hud)` runs `draw(const Sprite&)`, because each argument's type fits only one function. With no overlay entry each overload is unsafe to call, so `L3015` asks for `@safety` once per function, as for any imported function (verdicts 125, 134). With the overlay, `fn new(width, height)`, `fn draw(mesh)` and `fn draw(sprite)` each fit one function by count and parameter names, and entries are counted by function, so there is no `E5010`. Those three calls need no `unsafe`; `new()` stays unsafe.
answers.decides: FFI-39b's added sentence (p21-annex-c.md, after line 130): 'Each use of a C++ name of several functions … stands for the one it fits, ranked as `[TYP-24]` ranks instances …: a call (`new`, `super.init(…)`) by its object and its arguments' number, names, types and words'. TYP-26's added sentence (p04-types.md, after line 868) lifts `E1030`. The overlay is decided by FFI-12 (p16-ffi.md 322-323), by FFI-39b's 'an overlay entry by what it writes', and by GRM-35's added 'count entries by function' (after line 267).

sibling_cases.case: A renderer's shader uniforms: int/float overloads with the same parameter names, called with literals, vouched for in an overlay
sibling_cases.outcome: Compiles, with no `unsafe`. Each typed entry fits one function and is checked against it. `s.set(c"light_count", 4)` runs `set(const char*, int)`: the literal counts as C++'s `int`, `c_int`, which is an exact fit and wins over `f32`. `s.set(c"exposure", 1.5)` runs `set(const char*, float)`, the only one a float literal fits. Written as `fn set(name: borrowed nul_terminated, value)`, an entry fits both functions and is `E5010`, naming them.

sibling_cases.case: A game engine's asset cache: a copy/move pair (const T& and T&&) told apart by the word each call writes
sibling_cases.outcome: Compiles and prints `2048`. `cache.add(atlas)` runs `add(const Texture&)`, imported as `texture: Texture`: a plain argument fits only the parameter that reads, because the other one needs `owns`. `cache.add(owns splash)` runs `add(Texture&&)`, imported as `owns texture: Texture`, because `owns` before an argument fits no reading parameter. A further `cache.add(owns splash)` still picks `add(Texture&&)` by its words, and is `E3040` at that line ('`splash` was handed over on the line above'), not 'no function fits'.

sibling_cases.case: A server's config: a const/non-const accessor pair called through a changeable name and through a read-only one
sibling_cases.outcome: Compiles and prints `8080`, as C++ does. In `main`, `cfg` may be changed, so its object fits the `at` that changes it exactly and the const one only as a read-only view: `cfg.at(0).port = 8080` runs `Entry& at(size_t)`. In `port_of`, `cfg` only reads, so only `at(size_t) const` fits (the other would change it, E3023). The importer reads that the const `at` changes no field. Every function in the pair can be reached by some call.

sibling_cases.case: A UI toolkit's event handler: an Ember class overriding one of two overloads of a C++ virtual
sibling_cases.outcome: Compiles and prints `1`. By its parameter, `override fn on(e: gui.ui.KeyEvent)` fits only `on(const KeyEvent&)`, so the trampoline sends only that virtual slot to `Hotkeys.on`. `on(const MouseEvent&)` stays the base's, and the click runs it. A `MouseEvent` never reaches a function that takes a `KeyEvent` (in C++ terms, no virtual call lands in an override with another signature). An override whose parameters fit neither function, or both, is refused, naming them.

sibling_cases.case: A game engine's math library: an overloaded function stored as a function value
sibling_cases.outcome: Compiles and prints `32 32`. The value `vm.dot` stands for the function its expected type `fn(vm.Vec3i, vm.Vec3i) -> c_int` fits, `dot(Vec3i, Vec3i)`, as C++ picks an overload by the pointer type it is assigned to. The call `vm.dot(a, b)` picks the same function by its arguments. `f = vm.dot` with no expected type fits both equally and is `E2070`, naming them. The two entries differ only in types, so they write them.

readability.before: Today no rule lets the C++ program's own calls work: `r = eng.gfx.Renderer.new(1280, 720)`, `r.draw(mesh)`, `r.draw(hud)` (two `new` and two `draw` read as E1030). The workaround is a hand-written C++ shim with one name per overload, `draw_mesh(r, mesh)` and `draw_sprite(r, hud)`. In an overlay, `fn draw(mesh)` and `fn draw(sprite)` under `class Renderer:` hit 'a second entry for one name'.
readability.after: The same three lines compile unchanged, with C++'s own names and no new word at any call. Literals pick what C++ picks (`s.set(c"mode", 2)` runs the `int` overload), and a const/non-const accessor works through both kinds of name, so no `as c_int` and no helper function are needed. Overriding one overload is `override fn on(e: gui.ui.KeyEvent)`, as for any method. The overlay for overloads that differ in count or parameter names stays `fn draw(mesh)` / `fn draw(sprite)`. Only functions alike in every parameter name write the types, as Ember writes a parameter: `fn set(name: *c_char borrowed nul_terminated, value: f32)`.
readability.verdict: No longer and no harder. The ordinary program is shorter than today's shim. Extra words appear only on the rare overlay entry whose parameter names cannot say which function it vouches for.

final.cost: None at run time: it is decided when compiling. Each call is a direct call of the chosen function's thunk, just as a C++ call resolves its overload when compiling. Per call that is the same single thunk call as any imported C++ function, inlined across the boundary under the project's LTO. There is no table and no check while running. Compile time adds one fit test per candidate function at each use of an overloaded name (to measure).

verdicts_kept.verdict: 125: C++ functions stay unsafe until an overlay entry vouches for them (functions `import cpp` writes carry `@safety` in their entry)
verdicts_kept.how: Kept, and now followable for every overload. Each function has an entry of its own, told apart by count and names, or by the types GRM-35's sentence lets it write. So `@safety("…")` above `unsafe fn draw(mesh)` states the preconditions of exactly that overload. An overload no entry names stays unsafe to call, and its call is `L3015`, as before.

verdicts_kept.verdict: 131: C++ member lines go under their class
verdicts_kept.how: Kept. A member's overload entries are written under `class Renderer:`, and an entry is matched against that class's members only. A top-level entry naming only members stays `E5010`, with FFI-12's message. 131 removed one line vouching for two functions, and the new sentence refuses that for overloads too: an entry that fits several functions is `E5010`.

verdicts_kept.verdict: 132: an overlay entry without `@ffi(const)` makes its method one that changes its object
verdicts_kept.how: Kept, per function, and now also the thing that names one of a const/non-const pair. The entry's object counts as read-only with `@ffi(const)` and as changing without it. So `@ffi(const) fn visit(ref mut v: Visitor)` describes the const `visit` and `fn visit(ref mut v: Visitor)` the other, with no new word. An entry without it still makes its method one that changes its object. Nothing falls back to the importer's reading of a body when an entry exists.

verdicts_kept.verdict: 146 and 147: `owns` at the call for an `owns` parameter, and an error for `owns` before a parameter that only reads
verdicts_kept.how: Kept. The choice counts the words the call writes, and that is what tells `const T&` from `T&&`. Which words a call must write is unchanged; a word written wrongly fits no function. Whether verdict 159's 'a constructor's argument takes no word' reaches a C++ constructor is not decided here.

decisions.title: How a C++ name declared several times imports, and which function each use stands for
decisions.problem: C++ headers declare overloads and several constructors under one name, which Ember programs may not do. Nothing says what Ember name they get, or which function a call, an override, a function value or an overlay entry stands for. Only `super.init` picks a C++ constructor by its arguments. The compiler can work this out from each use, as C++ does, so no written word is needed. The choice is how the rule is stated, and whether the code around a call (unsafe code, effects, a value already handed over) may change which function it runs.

options.code:
r = eng.gfx.Renderer.new(1280, 720)   # Renderer(int, int)
r.draw(mesh)                           # draw(const Mesh&)
r.draw(hud)                            # draw(const Sprite&)
options.outcome: Compiles. There is one Ember name per C++ name. Each use stands for the function its own words fit: a call by its object and arguments, an override by its parameters, a function value by its expected type. Exact types are taken first. What the code around the use permits is checked afterwards, on that function. None, or two fitting equally, is an error naming each C++ declaration.

options.code:
r = eng.gfx.Renderer.new_int_int(1280, 720)
r.draw_Mesh(mesh)
r.draw_Sprite(hud)
options.outcome: Compiles. Each overload is its own Ember function, named from C++ types the program never wrote, and the names change when the header renames a type.

options.code:
unsafe overlay cpp "renderer.hpp":
    class Renderer:
        rename new(width, height) as sized
        rename draw(mesh) as draw_mesh
        rename draw(sprite) as draw_sprite
options.outcome: Without the overlay every overload is skipped, and `r.draw(mesh)` gives a 'skipped: overloaded' diagnostic. With it, `r.draw_mesh(mesh)` compiles. Today's `rename` grammar takes only a name, so the grammar would have to change too.

options.code:
ring.push(pcm)            # push(int32_t): the only one with an overlay entry
# SAFETY: push(int16_t) only stores the sample in the ring's own buffer
unsafe:
    ring.push(pcm)        # push(int16_t): the exact fit
options.outcome: Compiles, but the same line runs two different C++ functions. A call chooses among the functions it could compile as where it stands, so moving it into or out of an `unsafe:` block, or into a `@noalloc` function, silently changes which one runs.

decisions.parameters_in_order: 1. The three goals: A keeps C++'s names, adds no word and costs nothing while running. B and C add names the program must write or keep. 2. Safety: A runs one function per line wherever the line stands, and refuses a use that no function fits, or that two fit equally. D lets the surrounding code change what runs, with no diagnostic. 3. Compile time first: A is decided when compiling, as a direct call of the chosen thunk. 4. A written word only for meaning: B's type-built names and C's renames are bookkeeping. 5. The ordinary program: A is the C++ program's own lines. B is longer and breaks when a type is renamed. C needs an overlay line per overload before anything works. 6. Consistency: FFI-39b already picks `super.init`'s constructor by arity and argument types. TYP-24 already chooses among one name's interface instances by a call's arguments. FFI-48 refuses only overloads no call can tell apart. FFI-44 imports classes automatically, and FFI-40 and FFI-41 keep C++'s names. C++ chooses by the call alone, never by the code around it.
decisions.recommendation: A: FFI-39b's selection extended to every use of an overloaded C++ name, by the use's own words. TYP-26 states why a header's overloads are not the program's (principle 6).

owner_short.one_line: A C++ class with two constructors and two `draw(...)` overloads: what Ember calls them, and which one `r.draw(mesh)` runs.
owner_short.step_table:
| step | who | what happens | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | importer | reads `Renderer()`, `Renderer(int, int)`, `draw(const Mesh&)`, `draw(const Sprite&)` | one `new` and one `draw` on `Renderer` |
| 2 | program | writes `Renderer.new(1280, 720)` and `r.draw(mesh)` | no new word |
| 3 | compiler | keeps the functions the call's own words fit (count, names, types, `owns` / `ref mut`, the object) | `Renderer(int, int)`, `draw(const Mesh&)` |
| 4 | compiler | takes the exact fit; none, or still two, is an error naming each; then checks `unsafe` and the rest on that one | the same function wherever the line stands |
| 5 | program runs | a direct call of that function | the same cost as the C++ call |
owner_short.today: Nothing says. Read literally, two functions of one name are an error, and only `super.init` picks a C++ constructor by its arguments.
options: A: one name per C++ name; each use picks by its own words, as C++ does and as `super.init` already does
B: one name per overload, built from its types (`draw_Mesh`, `new_int_int`)
C: overloads skipped unless an overlay renames each one
D: as A, but a call picks among the functions it could compile as where it stands, so moving it into an `unsafe:` block can change which one runs
owner_short.recommendation: A: the C++ program's own calls work unchanged, one line always runs one function, and an unclear call is refused with the candidates named.

decisions.title: How an overlay entry names one of several C++ functions alike in name, parameter count and parameter names
decisions.problem: An overlay entry is matched by name, parameter count and parameter names (FFI-12), and contract words take the place of types (GRM-35). That tells apart overloads that differ in count or names, but not `set(const char* name, float value)` from `set(const char* name, int value)`. Which function an entry vouches for is meaning the compiler cannot guess, so the only choices are a written word or a refusal.

options.outcome: Compiles. One line makes both overloads safe to call, including one its writer may never have looked at, and both must take the same contract words.

Compiles. An entry may write a parameter's type and word as the import maps them, checked against the header. Each of these lines therefore names one function and is checked against it. The untyped line fits both and is E5010, naming both. Entries whose names already differ are written as today.
Refused, and no line can name either overload. Both stay unsafe to call, with no place to write their `@safety`.
Compiles. Each overload is named by C++ text in a string: a second spelling, in another language, of what a parameter list already says.

decisions.parameters_in_order: 1. The three goals: b keeps the overlay readable as Ember and costs nothing while running. 2. Safety: a lets one line vouch for a function its writer never named (verdict 131's problem). b, c and d refuse an entry that fits several functions. 3. Compile time first: all four are decided when compiling. 4. A written word only for meaning: which function a line vouches for is meaning. Under b the type is needed only where the names do not tell; elsewhere it is optional and checked. c makes it impossible to write, an exemption that exists only because syntax is missing (ODR 13's lesson). 5. The ordinary overlay: unchanged under b; d adds an attribute line per overload. 6. Consistency: b is Ember's own spelling of a parameter (`value: f32`, `owns value: Texture`), optional as a variable's type is, and overlays already write types in `@ffi(macro_fn)` entries (checklist 11). d is a second spelling. On 2026-10-29 the lead removed the separate typed member line ('one way to write an overlay line'); b keeps one entry form, whose parameters may carry a type.
decisions.departs_from_verdict: none (it refines the lead's ruling of 2026-10-29, decisions.md section 10, which removed the separate typed member line: here the one entry form may carry a parameter's type, checked against the header)
decisions.recommendation: b: an entry may write its parameters' and result's word and type as the import maps them, checked. An entry whose words still fit several functions is E5010, naming them.

owner_short.one_line: Two C++ overloads with the same parameter names, `set(const char* name, float value)` and `set(const char* name, int value)`: how an overlay line says which one it vouches for.
owner_short.step_table:
| step | who | what happens | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | overlay writer | writes `fn set(name: borrowed nul_terminated, value)` | it fits both overloads |
| 2 | compiler | refuses it, naming both C++ declarations | error |
| 3 | overlay writer | writes `fn set(name: *c_char borrowed nul_terminated, value: f32)`, and the same line with `value: c_int` | each line names one overload |
| 4 | compiler | checks each line against its own overload, as for any entry | both overloads safe to call |
owner_short.today: Overlay lines are matched by name, count and parameter names only, so such a pair cannot be told apart, and a second line for one name is an error.
options: a: one line covers every overload it fits
b: the line may write the parameters' Ember types, as Ember writes a function's first line, and must where the names do not tell
c: refuse, with no way to vouch for either overload
d: write the C++ signature in an attribute, `@ffi(cpp="set(const char*, float)")`
owner_short.recommendation: b: Ember's own spelling of a parameter, needed only where the names do not already tell the overloads apart.

decisions.title: Which overload an untyped number literal picks
decisions.problem: Among overloads that differ in a number type, Ember's ranking takes exact types first, counting a literal as its default type. Ember's defaults are a 64-bit `int` and `f64`. C's `int` is never Ember's `int`, so `s.set(c"mode", 2)` beside `set(const char*, int)` and `set(const char*, float)` reaches both only by conversion, and is refused. `super.init(16, 8)` beside `Widget(int, int)` and `Widget(float, float)` is refused too. The compiler cannot know from the header alone which type a literal 'is'; this is a choice of rule.

options.code:
s.set(c"mode", 2)            # error: `2` counts as Ember's `int` (i64); both `set` reach it by conversion
s.set(c"mode", 2 as c_int)   # what the program must write
options.outcome: Refused, with `as c_int` to write on every literal call of an int/float overload pair; `super.init(16, 8)` too.

options.code:
s.set(c"mode", 2)            # set(const char*, int): a whole-number literal prefers whole-number types
out.put(5)                   # error: put(int) and put(long) both take whole numbers
m.scale(2.0)                 # error: scale(float) and scale(double) both take floats
options.outcome: Compiles for `set`. Refuses the int/long and float/double pairs, which C++ calls without trouble.

options.code:
s.set(c"mode", 2)            # set(const char*, int): `2` counts as C++'s `int`
out.put(5)                   # put(int)
m.scale(2.0)                 # scale(double): `2.0` is C++'s `double`
w.value(7)                   # error, as in C++: value(int64_t) and value(double) both convert
options.outcome: Compiles wherever C++ picks one, running the same function. Refused, naming both, where C++ is ambiguous too.

decisions.parameters_in_order: 1. The three goals: iii keeps the C++ program's lines with no cast and costs nothing while running. 2. Safety: all three are decided when compiling and refuse rather than guess. iii never runs a different function from C++, because Ember's exact fit is C++'s and Ember's conversions are fewer. 3. Compile time first: all three. 4. A written word only for meaning: i's `as c_int` on every literal is bookkeeping, and so are the casts ii needs. 5. The ordinary program: under iii it is the C++ line. i and ii refuse common calls (uniforms, int/long, float/double). 6. Consistency: when choosing among one name's instances, the nearest rule (TYP-24) already counts a literal as its default type. iii does exactly that, with the defaults of the language the header is written in (`int`, `double`).
decisions.recommendation: iii: when choosing among C++ overloads, an untyped literal counts as C++ types it (`c_int`, `f64`).

owner_short.one_line: C++ `set(const char* name, int value)` and `set(const char* name, float value)`: which one `s.set(c"mode", 2)` runs.
owner_short.step_table:
| step | who | what happens | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | program | writes `s.set(c"mode", 2)` | a plain `2` |
| 2 | compiler | counts `2` as C++ counts it, an `int` | |
| 3 | compiler | `set(…, int)` takes it as it is, `set(…, float)` only by conversion | `set(const char*, int)` |
| 4 | compiler | where C++ itself cannot choose (`value(int64_t)` / `value(double)` with `7`), an error naming both | `7 as i64` picks one |
owner_short.today: Nothing says. Read as Ember's other overload choice, `2` counts as Ember's 64-bit `int`, which neither function takes, so the call is an error.
options: i: count a literal as Ember's default (64-bit `int`, `f64`): `s.set(c"mode", 2)` is an error; write `2 as c_int`
ii: a whole-number literal prefers any whole-number type: `set` works, but `put(int)` / `put(long)` with `5`, and `scale(float)` / `scale(double)` with `2.0`, are errors
iii: count a literal as C++ does (`int`, `double`): Ember runs what C++ runs, and refuses where C++ refuses
owner_short.recommendation: iii: the C++ lines work unchanged and never run a different function from the one C++ would.

decisions.title: Which of a const and a non-const C++ method a call runs
decisions.problem: C++ classes pair `const Entry& at(size_t) const` with `Entry& at(size_t)`. Through a name that only reads, only the const one can be called (a method that may change its object is E3023). Through a changeable name both can be called with the same arguments, so ranking by arguments alone ties. The tie refuses every call, and the non-const `at` could then never be called by any line.

options.code: cfg.at(0).port = 8080      # error: both `at` fit a changeable `cfg` equally
options.outcome: Refused through every changeable name, which is the ordinary local. No line can ever call `Entry& at`.

options.code:
cfg.at(0).port = 8080      # Entry& at(size_t): `cfg` may be changed
# in fn port_of(cfg: net.srv.Config):
return cfg.at(0).port      # const Entry& at(size_t) const: `cfg` only reads
options.outcome: Compiles and runs what C++ runs. The non-const result is a changing view of `cfg` while it is used, as C++'s `Entry&` is, so two such results held at once through one changeable name are refused.

options.code:
e = cfg.at(0)              # const at: the result is only read
cfg.at(0).port = 8080      # Entry& at: the result is changed
options.outcome: Compiles more Ember programs, but which C++ function a call runs depends on the lines after it, and can differ from C++. For example, a copy-on-write string's non-const accessor copies and the const one does not.

decisions.parameters_in_order: 1. The three goals: b keeps C++'s meaning with no word and no run-time cost. 2. Safety: b and c are safe, but c runs a different function from C++ for the same call; a refuses. 3. Compile time first: all three. 4. A written word only for meaning: none of them needs one. a needs a helper function to reach the const `at` through a changeable name, and leaves the other `at` unreachable, an exemption that exists only because syntax is missing (ODR 13's lesson). 5. The ordinary program: b compiles the C++ lines; a refuses them. 6. Consistency: the object counts as one more argument under the nearest rule (exact before coercion; a read-only view of a changeable place is a coercion, TYP-5 rule 7), as C++ counts its implied object. An overlay entry's `@ffi(const)` (verdict 132) then names which of the pair it describes, with no new word. c would choose by the code around the call, which the first decision excludes. K47 (J8-05) keeps its own question, the overlay name of `operator[]`, whose pair goes through Index/IndexMut (FFI-42), not this selection.
decisions.recommendation: b: the object is ranked as an argument, `ref` through a name that only reads it or in an entry with `@ffi(const)`, `ref mut` otherwise, so a changeable name picks the non-const method and a read-only one the const method, as in C++.

owner_short.one_line: C++ `const Entry& at(size_t) const` and `Entry& at(size_t)`: which one `cfg.at(0)` runs.
owner_short.step_table:
| step | who | what happens | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | program | writes `cfg.at(0).port = 8080` in `main`, where `cfg` may be changed | no new word |
| 2 | compiler | the non-const `at` fits `cfg` as it is, the const one only as a read-only view | `Entry& at(size_t)` |
| 3 | compiler | in `port_of(cfg: Config)`, `cfg` only reads, so only the const `at` fits | `const Entry& at(size_t) const` |
| 4 | program runs | prints `8080` | as in C++ |
owner_short.today: Nothing says. Read literally, two functions of one name are an error.
options: a: both fit a changeable name equally: an error, and the non-const `at` can never be called
b: as in C++: a changeable name picks the non-const `at`, a read-only one the const `at`
c: the const `at` unless the result is changed, as Rust picks between its two indexing interfaces
owner_short.recommendation: b: what C++ runs, decided by the call alone, and every function in the pair can be called.

Redeclaration: a member declared in its class and defined below it, or a function declared twice, is one function (one USR). No `E2070` and no `E5010`.

Overlay record: the renderer overlay gives no `E5010`. `ember.overlays` keys each entry by its function (the key format is the lead's tooling). A new overload whose parameter has the same name makes the old entry `E5010`, naming both.

Const pair in an overlay: `@ffi(const) fn visit(ref mut v: Visitor)` describes the const `visit` and `fn visit(ref mut v: Visitor)` the other; `root.visit(ref mut tally)` through a read-only `root` runs the const one.
Typed entries: how a type named like a contract word (`handle`, `one`, `status`) is read before the contract words. The lead decides the reading, for example a raw identifier `r#handle`.
`L3015` for an overloaded C++ name comes once per function and names every other call. Its message gives an entry line that compiles, with types where the names do not tell the functions apart.

`E2070`'s message for an imported overload set (the code table says 'ambiguous interface method') is the lead's wording. It names each C++ declaration and why each does not fit; where all fail for one reason (E3023 for every overload), it gives that reason.
Whether `c_int` and `c_long` are distinct Ember types on MSVC (pre-existing, E1-12). If they are aliases, `put(int)` / `put(long)` import with one signature and every call ties.
final.notes:
Outcome reasoning. As in the first answer, the call selection comes from properties the specification already has:
- FFI-39b picks a C++ constructor by arity and argument types.
- TYP-24 ranks one name's instances exact before coercion, with ties as E2070.
- FFI-48's row refuses only the overloads no call can tell apart, which presumes the others import.
- FFI-44, FFI-40 and FFI-41 keep C++'s names.
So options B and C contradict the specification. The repair keeps all of that. It answers the breakers' three causes with one property: every use of such a name (a call, an override, a function value, an overlay entry) stands for the one function it fits. The fit is ranked as TYP-24 ranks, with C++'s literal types and C++'s treatment of the object, and whatever the code around the use permits is checked on the chosen function. The repair edits the same three rules as the first answer. It needs four choices, all recorded in decisions for the owner's later review: the selection, the typed entry, literals, and the const/non-const pair. Hence decided_by_parameters. Nothing goes into the specification before that review.

Triage: 18 holes are real, caused by the first edit's own words, and 2 are pre-existing (E1-11, E1-12). E1-10 was filed as pre_existing by its breaker, but it is S1-3's program and cause, so it is counted as real. Its E2070 comes from the edit's own tie rule, on a program the edit says it makes work, not from TYP-26's E1030.

Left alone, because they are outside the allowed rules or pre-existing:
(1) FFI-30c's words still say 'for one name'. GRM-35's added sentence says FFI-30c and FFI-55 count entries by function; the lead may align FFI-30c's own words in the hardening.
(2) FFI-48's row says 'rename one in the overlay', but `rename` and `hide` take only a name (pre-existing). An overlay `extend` wrapper (FFI-13) can give one overload a name of its own.
(3) CLS-4's 'A method named like an inherited one replaces it' is not edited. FFI-39b's 'an `override fn` by its parameters' decides which function it replaces for a C++ name. Whether IV.11's nearest-first lookup still lets Ember code reach the base's other overloads through the derived class is listed to verify.
(4) E1-11: an Ember class that overrides two overloads of one C++ virtual writes two methods of one name, which is E1030 under TYP-26 with or without the edit. It is a gap for the list.
(5) E1-12: whether `c_int` and `c_long` are distinct types (FFI-8).
(6) Not stated anywhere:
- how C++ copy and move constructors import;
- whether C++ default arguments import (if they do, `f(a)` against `f(a, b = 0)` ties, as in C++);
- C++ name hiding between a base and a derived class;
- a const/non-const pair of virtual methods overridden in Ember. An Ember method's change of `this` is worked out from its body, so the override fits both by parameters and is refused, naming both.
(7) Whether verdict 159 reaches C++ constructors is not decided here.
(8) K47 (J8-05, the overlay name of `operator[]`) keeps its question. Decision 4 settles the const/non-const choice for ordinary method calls only; `operator[]` pairs go through Index/IndexMut (FFI-42).

Nothing was run, and every claim that would need a run is in to_verify. Per the rules, characters were not counted; the repair was written to be shorter than the first answer, and the script's measure decides.

triage.evidence: Under the edit both `draw` import (TYP-26's added sentence), and FFI-39b's added sentence picks only for 'Every call'. Overrides are still decided by name: CLS-4 (p05-declarations.md 335-338) says 'A method named like an inherited one replaces it', and FFI-39 (p21-annex-c.md 122-124) says the trampoline 'passes on to the Ember class exactly the virtual methods it overrides (`override fn`)'. So which slot `Button.draw` takes is undecided, and one reading is both. That reading sends a `Label` into code that reads a `Mesh`. Without the edit the base is E1030 (p04-types.md 867-868) and nothing can derive from it.

The added words choose 'of the declarations it would compile as a call of'. FFI-2 (p16-ffi.md 40-41) says 'A header function with no overlay entry therefore stays unsafe to call', so outside `unsafe:` only `push(int32_t)` compiles, reached by widening (TYP-5 rule 1, p04-types.md 74). Inside `unsafe:` both compile and the exact one wins. The same line runs two different functions. Without the edit the name is E1030.

Through the changeable local `cfg`, both `at` compile (FFI-40, p21-annex-c.md 156-163) with the same `usize` parameter, so the added 'several fitting equally, is `E2070`' refuses both lines. E2070's way out is `I[A].m(recv, …)` (p04-types.md 566), and there is no interface here. `rename` and `hide` take only a name (p16-ffi.md 257). So no line reaches `Entry& at`. The refusal comes from the edit's own tie rule, on a program its intent says it makes work, not from TYP-26's E1030.

TYP-24 (p04-types.md 563-565) chooses with 'an untyped literal counting as its default type (`int`, `f64`)', and `int` is `i64` (p04-types.md 32). LEX-16 (p02-lexical.md 139-141) lets `4` reach both `c_int` and `f32`, so both are reached 'only through a coercion' and the call ties: E2070. C++ calls `set(const char*, int)`, an exact match. The refusal comes from the edit's borrowed ranking.

FFI-30c (p16-ffi.md 221-222) says 'any other second entry for one name is `E5010`'. The added GRM-35 sentence says 'a second entry (`[FFI-30c]`) count by declaration'. So two rules give opposite verdicts on the question's own overlay. Low severity: the wrong reading is a refusal.

FFI-39b's added sentence decides only 'Every call', and `sink: fn(c_int) = lg.logx.write` is not a call. TYP-5 rule 10 (p04-types.md 88) and CLO-3 (p06-expressions.md 255-258) fill a callable 'from a named function', and that name now stands for two functions. Nothing picks one.

The added words count 'a C++ name declared more than once in one scope' and 'declarations'. An in-class declaration plus its out-of-class definition is two declarations of one function. FFI-30 (p16-ffi.md 206-209) merges by USR only 'Two imports of one C declaration', so read literally the call ties. Low severity: a careful reader merges them.

The fit is 'would compile'. At the second `cache.add(owns splash)`, `splash` was handed over, so neither function compiles (E3040, and E3028 for the reading one). The added 'none … is `E2070`' then gives E2070, whose table row is 'ambiguous interface method' (p17a-codes.md 67), instead of E3040 at the line.

This is S1-4's cause. `2` counts as `i64` (TYP-24, p04-types.md 563-565; p04-types.md 32), and both `c_int` and `f32` are reached through LEX-16 (p02-lexical.md 139-141), so the call is E2070. FFI-39b today picks `super.init` 'by arity and argument types' (p21-annex-c.md 128-129), and C++ picks `(int, int)` for two integer literals. The added sentence makes `super.init(16, 8)` E2070 instead.

This is S1-2's cause. 'the declarations it would compile as a call of' leaves open whether unsafe code filters the candidates (E3100, p09-memory.md 269-275). Under one reading the line runs `gain(float)` outside `unsafe:` and `gain(double)` inside it; under the other the call is steered to the unsafe overload. The words allow both readings.

This is S1-6's cause. FN-6 (p05-declarations.md 175) says 'A function is a value', and CLO-3 (p06-expressions.md 255-258) fills a callable 'from a named function'. The added sentence chooses only for 'every call', so `vm.dot` used as a value is undecided.

This is S1-1's cause. CLS-4 (p05-declarations.md 336-338) replaces 'by name', and FFI-39 (p21-annex-c.md 121-125) passes on 'exactly the virtual methods it overrides'. Which of the two inherited `on` the override replaces is undecided, and one reading routes a `MouseEvent` into a function that takes a `KeyEvent`.
This is S1-5's cause. FFI-30c (p16-ffi.md 221-222) is unchanged and still says E5010 for 'any other second entry for one name', against GRM-35's added 'count by declaration'.

FFI-55's record keys one fingerprint per name (p16-ffi.md 336-340: `SDL_FreeSurface = "blake3:…"`), so two entries of one name share one key. The refusal of the unchanged `fn draw(mesh)` once a second `mesh` overload appears is the safe result and follows from the entry rule; the hole is the record's key per name. Low severity.

Both `visit` import as `visit(ref mut v: Visitor)` with no result (FFI-40, p21-annex-c.md 161-163). The added GRM-35 typed form writes only parameters and result, which are the same for both, so each entry 'still fits several' and is E5010. `@ffi(const)` (p16-ffi.md 271-273) asserts a fact; it does not match a declaration. Neither overload can then carry an entry or `@safety`, which the edit's own decision b said every overload could.

The added sentence allows the typed form only 'where its name, parameter count and parameter names fit several declarations', and changes no production. `overlay_param := IDENT [":" contract {contract}]` (p16-ffi.md 262) still reads `Vec3i` and `c_int` as contract words. So when a typed entry may be written, and how it parses, are both open. Low severity.
This is S1-7's cause. 'declared more than once in one scope' counts redeclarations, which FFI-30 (p16-ffi.md 206-209) treats as one entity only through a cross-reading. Low severity.

It is S1-3's program and cause. `cfg` is a changeable local, both `at` compile with the same `usize`, and the added 'several fitting equally, is `E2070`' refuses the call. The first answer's own to_verify says 'as these words decide'. The refusal comes from the edit's tie rule, not from TYP-26's E1030, so it is not the same fault without the edit.

The class's own two `override fn on` are 'two functions of one name in one scope' (TYP-26, p04-types.md 867-868), which is E1030 with or without the edit. The edit's sentence covers only the header's declarations. This is a new gap for the list: an Ember class overriding each overload of a C++ virtual.

FFI-8 (p16-ffi.md 173) maps `int`, `long` and `long long` to `c_int`, `c_long` and `i64` without saying whether `c_int` and `c_long` are distinct types. On MSVC the `put(int)` / `put(long)` pair would have one Ember signature under any selection rule, so it fails the same way without the edit.

causes.cause: The edit spoke of 'every call' and of 'declarations'. The language uses a function's name in more ways than a call (an `override fn`, a function value, an overlay entry, and the overlay rules that count entries), and it counts functions, not their redeclarations. So every use other than a call still read one name as one function, and a redeclaration read as an overload.
The fit was 'the declarations it would compile as a call of', so everything that decides whether a line compiles (unsafe code, effects, a value already handed over) also decided which function runs.

The ranking took TYP-24's Ember defaults and left the object out. A literal counted as `i64`, which no C type is, and an object behind a changeable name fit a const and a non-const method equally. So the choice differed from C++'s exactly where C++ picks one, and some functions could never be reached.

holes_left.today: Refused, read literally: Handler's two `on` are 'two functions of one name in one scope' (TYP-26, p04-types.md 867-868, E1030), so `class KeyLog(gui.ui.Handler)` binds to nothing.
holes_left.with_edit: TYP-26's added sentence imports both `on` as one name. FFI-39b's added sentence picks what an `override fn` stands for 'by its parameters', 'ranked as [TYP-24] ranks instances': an exact fit first, else one 'the arguments reach only through a coercion' (TYP-24, p04-types.md 563-566). `e: gui.ui.KeyEvent` does not fit `on(int timer_id)`. It fits `on(const Event& e)` through a coercion, the upcast of TYP-5 rule 8 (p04-types.md 84-86). That is the only fit, so it is chosen, and the trampoline sends the `on(const Event&)` slot to `KeyLog.on` (FFI-39, p21-annex-c.md 121-125; DSP-2, p08-classes.md 287: 'an override reuses the base's slot'). 'What the code around it permits is checked after' covers unsafe code, effects, values handed over, threads and views, not the override's own parameter type, and no rule compares an override's parameters with the method it replaces (CLS-4, p05-declarations.md 335-339). It compiles.
holes_left.what_goes_wrong: `send_focus` calls `h.on(FocusEvent())`. The slot runs `KeyLog.on` with a FocusEvent taken as a KeyEvent, and `e.code()`, which the overlay vouches safe and which is true for a real KeyEvent, reads `code_` at offset 8 of an 8-byte object. In C++ terms this is an unchecked `static_cast` downcast, a read past the object, and it happens in safe Ember code: both `unsafe:` notes are true. C++ itself refuses this class ('marked override but does not override'). The scalar case goes wrong the same way: `override fn on(timer_id: i16)` fits `on(int)` by widening, so C++'s 70000 reaches an `i16` truncated, while the safe direction, `override fn on(timer_id: int)`, fits nothing. For an override the coercion runs backwards, because C++'s argument flows into the Ember parameter.

holes_left.with_edit: TYP-24 has only two tiers. An instance whose parameter types are the arguments' own is chosen before one reached 'only through a coercion', and 'arguments that fit two equally are E2070' (p04-types.md 563-566; RNG-5a2 p04-types.md 236-237: 'exactly before considering any coercion'). The loop's `slot` is an `int` that reaches `c_int` only by rule 12 (p04-types.md 92-99), for both `set`. So both are in the coercion tier, even though `4` (counted as `c_int`) is exact for one: E2070. In `scene.light(0)`, `0` counts as `c_int` and reaches `usize` by literal typing (LEX-16, p02-lexical.md 139-141) for both `light`. The object's exact fit (`ref mut`) does not lift the non-const one out of the coercion tier: E2070 on both lines. The answer's config sibling (`cfg.at(0).port = 8080`) is E2070 the same way, not '8080'.
holes_left.what_goes_wrong: C++ ranks argument by argument: set(int, int) beats set(int, float) on the second argument and ties on the first, and the non-const `light` beats the const one on the object. Ember refuses both ordinary lines. The same refusal hits every index call of a const/non-const accessor with a literal or an `int` index, and every pair where one shared argument needs a widening. The way out is a cast on each argument (`slot as c_int`, `0 as usize`), the bookkeeping decisions 1 and 4 say the edit removes. S1-3's own program (`cfg.at(0).port = 8080`) is still refused, so S1-3 and E1-10 are not repaired. The same cause ties a nearer base against a farther one (`draw(const Shape&)` / `draw(const Circle&)` with a FilledCircle) and a promotion against a conversion (`put(int)` / `put(long)` with an `i16`), both of which C++ picks.

holes_left.today: Refused, read literally: two `at` are E1030 (TYP-26, p04-types.md 867-868), and the second entry is E5010 (FFI-30c, p16-ffi.md 221-222).
holes_left.with_edit: The added sentence ranks the use's object, `ref` through a read-only name or in an entry with `@ffi(const)` and `ref mut` otherwise, against each candidate's object. It does not say what a candidate's object is: C++'s `const`, or what FFI-40 imports. FFI-40 (p21-annex-c.md 156-161) and FFI-40a (p21-annex-c.md 164-171) import a `const` method as only reading 'only when the body changes no field', and as changing it 'when the header does not have the body'. Under the import's reading both `at` change their object (`ref mut`). `@ffi(const) fn at(i)` (object `ref`) then fits neither, which is E5010, and `fn at(i)` fits both equally, which is E5010 too. With no overlay, `cfg.at(first)` fits both equally through `cfg` (E2070) and neither through `port_of`'s read-only `cfg`. Under C++'s `const`, it compiles and prints 8080.
holes_left.what_goes_wrong: Under the import's reading no line can call either `at`, unsafe code included, and no overlay line can vouch for either. That is the exemption that exists only because a word is missing (checklist 12). Bodies in a .cpp are the usual case for a non-template class. A `mutable` member (a cache, a mutex) in a const method is common too, and FFI-40a reads it as changing as well. E1-7's program (`visit` declared without a body) fails the same way, so E1-7 is not repaired. The answer's config sibling works only because its bodies are in the header ('The importer reads that the const `at` changes no field').
holes_left.rule_lines: FFI-39b added sentence ('an object as `ref` ... in an entry with `@ffi(const)`, else `ref mut`', 'an overlay entry by what it writes'); FFI-40 p21-annex-c.md 156-161; FFI-40a p21-annex-c.md 164-177; GRM-35 p16-ffi.md 271-273
holes_left.fix_hint: Which of a const and a non-const C++ method a use or an entry names is read from C++'s `const`; what the chosen one may do to its object is decided after, by its entry or the importer.

holes_left.today: Refused, read literally: two `at` are E1030 (TYP-26, p04-types.md 867-868); otherwise undecided.
holes_left.with_edit: The object counts 'as `ref` through a name that only reads it ..., else `ref mut`'. Inside `port`, whether `this` only reads is worked out from `port`'s body (CLS-7, p05-declarations.md 357-360; FN-4 p05-declarations.md 153-156), and that body is this very call. If the non-const `at` is chosen, `port` changes `this.cfg`, so `this` is changeable, which is consistent. If the const `at` is chosen, `port` only reads, so `this` is read-only, which is also consistent. The words allow both, so neither which C++ function runs nor whether `port` changes its object is decided.
holes_left.what_goes_wrong: Under the first answer `show(s: Server)` is E3023 ('`port` may change its object'). Under the second it compiles and prints 0. The same program compiles on one implementation and not on another, and runs a different C++ function, which matters wherever the pair differs (copy-on-write detaching, or a const accessor that is thread-safe beside a non-const one that is not). C++ decides by the method's own `const`, which Ember does not write. A lambda using a real variable (`fn() => println(cfg.at(i).port)`, CLO-2) is circular the same way. Wrapping a C++ object in an Ember class field is an ordinary pattern.

out.intent: Build a C++ renderer with its (width, height) constructor, then draw a mesh and a sprite through its two `draw` overloads, running the overloads the C++ header means.

existing_rule.words: `super.init(…)` selects the C++ base constructor by arity and argument types and runs it at `super.init(…)` (`[CLS-11]`)

edits.before: There is no overloading: two functions of one name in one scope are `E1030`, except operator-interface implementations and `extend` blocks for different types.
edits.after: A C++ header's declarations of one name import as that name, a call choosing among them (`[FFI-39b]`): the header, not the program, declares them, and a call tells them apart as it tells an interface's instances apart (`[TYP-24]`).
edits.why_general: States why the no-overloading rule does not reach a foreign header (principle 6: refusing it would refuse a correct program for code it did not write and cannot change), and that the choice is the one the language already makes among an interface's instances, so it is not a second kind of overloading. It reaches every C++ name declared more than once: namespace functions, methods, static functions, constructors, without naming one.

edits.before: `super.init(…)` selects the C++ base constructor by arity and argument types and runs it at `super.init(…)` (`[CLS-11]`); a base with no default constructor and no declared `init` is `E5058`.
edits.after: Every call of a C++ name declared more than once in one scope, constructors (`new`) and `super.init(…)` included, selects so: of the declarations it would compile as a call of, each taken alone (its object, and its arguments' number, names, types after coercions and words), it runs the one `[TYP-24]` would choose among an interface's instances; none, or several fitting equally, is `E2070`, naming each.
edits.why_general: Extends the selection FFI-39b already makes for `super.init` to every call of an overloaded C++ name, by the property every call already has (it is checked against one declaration) plus TYP-24's exact-before-coercion choice. With nothing added it decides constructors, methods and namespace functions; value overloads (`i64` against `f64` against `bool`); the `const T&` / `T&&` and `const T&` / `T&` pairs, told apart by the words a call writes (verdicts 146, 147); a method that changes its object called through a read-only name (E3023, so only the reading one fits); and refuses, naming the candidates, what no call can tell apart.

edits.before: In an entry marked `@ffi(macro_fn)` (`[FFI-6b]`) a parameter's and the result's words are one Ember type each (`IDENT ":" type`, `"->" type`), since a macro has no C declaration to read (ODR-147).
edits.after: An entry describes one declaration: where its name, parameter count and parameter names fit several declarations of one C++ name, it writes each parameter and the result as `[FFI-8]` and `[FFI-40]` map them, word and type (`ref mut v: Vec3`, `-> ref f32`), before any contract word; `override` and a second entry (`[FFI-30c]`) count by declaration, and one that still fits several is `E5010` (`[FFI-12]`), naming them.
edits.why_general: An entry vouches for exactly one declaration, as verdict 131 requires of a member line. Where name, count and parameter names already single one out (the question's own overlay) nothing changes; where they do not, the entry writes the parameters as Ember spells a function's first line, the form overlays already use for `@ffi(macro_fn)` entries. It reaches value overloads alike in names, reference-kind pairs, pointer overloads that need contract words, and pairs that differ only in their result, and makes `override` and the second-entry rule count per declaration for every overloaded name.

answers.question: J8-04
answers.today: Undecided, and refused if read literally. FFI-39b (p21-annex-c.md 128-129) selects a C++ constructor by arity and argument types only for `super.init`; nothing says which `new` or `draw` a call runs. TYP-26 (p04-types.md 867-868) makes `Renderer`'s two `new` and two `draw` 'two functions of one name in one scope', `E1030`. In the overlay, FFI-12 tells the two `draw` entries apart by their parameter names, but FFI-30c (p16-ffi.md 221-222) makes 'any other second entry for one name' `E5010`.
answers.after: Compiles. `Renderer.new(1280, 720)` runs `Renderer(int, int)`, the only constructor taking two arguments (the literals take `c_int`). `r.draw(mesh)` runs `draw(const Mesh&)` and `r.draw(hud)` runs `draw(const Sprite&)`: each is the only declaration its argument's type fits. With no overlay entry each overload is unsafe to call, so `L3015` asks for `@safety` as for any imported function (verdicts 125, 134). With the overlay, `fn new(width, height)`, `fn draw(mesh)` and `fn draw(sprite)` each describe one declaration, by count and names, and count by declaration, so there is no `E5010`. Those three need no `unsafe`; `new()` stays unsafe.
answers.decides: FFI-39b's added sentence (p21-annex-c.md, after line 130): 'Every call of a C++ name declared more than once in one scope, constructors (`new`) ... included, selects so ...'. TYP-26's added sentence (p04-types.md, after line 868) lifts `E1030`. The overlay is decided by FFI-12 (p16-ffi.md 322-323) and GRM-35's added sentence (after line 267: 'An entry describes one declaration ... count by declaration').

sibling_cases.case: A parser's JSON writer: one method, overloads by value type (int64_t, double, bool); literals and widening
sibling_cases.outcome: Compiles. `w.value(count)` runs `value(int64_t)`, the argument's own type. `w.value(7)` runs `value(int64_t)`: the literal counts as `int` (`i64`), chosen before `double`, which it reaches only as a float. `w.value(small)` runs `value(int64_t)`, the only declaration an `i32` reaches, by widening. `w.value(0.25)` runs `value(double)`, since a float literal fits no integer. `w.value(true)` runs `value(bool)`.

sibling_cases.case: A game engine's asset cache: copy/move pair (const T& against T&&) told apart by the word the call writes
sibling_cases.outcome: Compiles. `cache.add(atlas)` runs `add(const Texture&)`, imported as `texture: Texture`: a plain argument fits only the parameter that reads, since `owns` is required for the other (E3028). `atlas` stays usable. `cache.add(owns splash)` runs `add(Texture&&)`, imported as `owns texture: Texture`; `owns` before an argument for a reading parameter is an error, so only this one fits. `splash` ends, and a later use of it is `E3040`.

sibling_cases.case: A renderer's shader uniforms: overloads alike in name, count and parameter names, vouched in an overlay
sibling_cases.outcome: Compiles, with no `unsafe`. Each `set` entry writes its parameters as the import maps them, so it describes one declaration; both are checked against the header and counted by declaration. `s.set(c"tint", 0.5)` runs `set(const char*, float)`, since a float literal fits no `c_int`. `s.set(c"mode", mode)` runs `set(const char*, int)`. Written `fn set(name: borrowed nul_terminated, value)`, the entry fits both declarations and is `E5010`, naming them.

sibling_cases.case: A server's config: const/non-const accessor pair called through a read-only parameter
sibling_cases.outcome: Compiles, and `cfg.at(0)` runs `at(size_t) const`. `cfg` only reads, and the other `at` may change its object (E3023), so only the const one compiles as the call. The importer reads that the const `at` changes no field. Through a name that may change the config, both compile and fit equally, so the call is `E2070`, naming both. That pair is K47's question, asked after this one.

readability.before: Today no rule makes the C++ program's own calls work: `r = eng.gfx.Renderer.new(1280, 720)`, `r.draw(mesh)`, `r.draw(hud)` (two `new` and two `draw` read as E1030). The way round is a hand-written C++ shim with one name per overload, `draw_mesh(r, mesh)`, `draw_sprite(r, hud)`. In an overlay, `fn draw(mesh)` and `fn draw(sprite)` under `class Renderer:` hit 'a second entry for one name'.
readability.after: The same three lines compile unchanged, with C++'s own names and no new word at any call. The overlay for overloads that differ in parameter count or names stays `fn draw(mesh)` / `fn draw(sprite)`. Only overloads alike in every parameter name write the types, as Ember writes a first line: `fn set(name: *c_char borrowed nul_terminated, value: f32)`.
readability.verdict: No longer and no harder. The ordinary program is shorter than today's shim, and the extra words fall only on the rare overlay entry whose names cannot say which overload it vouches for.

out.cost: none: decided when compiling. Each call is a direct call of the chosen overload's thunk, as a C++ call resolves its overload when compiling: per call, the same one thunk call as any imported C++ function, inlined across the boundary under the project's LTO. There is no table and no check while running. Compile time adds one fit test per candidate declaration at each call of an overloaded name (to measure).

verdicts_kept.verdict: 125: C++ members stay unsafe until an overlay entry vouches (functions `import cpp` writes carry `@safety` in their entry)
verdicts_kept.how: Kept and made followable for every overload. Each declaration now has an entry of its own (by count and names, or by the types GRM-35's sentence writes), so `@safety("…")` above `unsafe fn draw(mesh)` states the preconditions of exactly that overload. An overload no entry names stays unsafe to call, and its call is `L3015`, as before.

verdicts_kept.verdict: 131: C++ member lines go under their class
verdicts_kept.how: Kept. Overload entries of a member are written under `class Renderer:`, and the new sentence chooses a declaration among that class's members only. A top-level entry naming only members stays `E5010` with FFI-12's message. One line vouching for two functions is what 131 removed, and the new sentence refuses it for overloads too: an entry that fits several declarations is `E5010`.

verdicts_kept.verdict: 132: an overlay entry without `@ffi(const)` makes its method one that changes its object
verdicts_kept.how: Kept, per declaration. Each overload's entry carries or omits `@ffi(const)` for itself, and one without it imports that overload as changing its object. The selection then counts that overload as a correct call only through a name that may change the object (E3023 otherwise). Nothing falls back to the importer's reading of a body when an entry exists.

verdicts_kept.verdict: 146 and 147: `owns` at the call for an `owns` parameter, and an error before a parameter that only reads
verdicts_kept.how: Kept. The selection only counts whether a call compiles against each declaration, and the words a call writes are part of that, which is what tells `const T&` from `T&&` apart. Which words a call must write is unchanged; whether verdict 159's 'a constructor's argument takes no word' reaches a C++ constructor is not decided here.

decisions.title: How a C++ name declared several times imports, and which declaration a call runs
decisions.problem: C++ headers declare overloads and several constructors under one name, and Ember programs may not (TYP-26). Nothing says what Ember name they get or how a call picks one; only `super.init` selects a C++ constructor 'by arity and argument types' (FFI-39b), and only overloads differing in return type are refused (FFI-48). The compiler can work the choice out from each call, as C++ does, so no written word is needed. The choice is how the spec states it.

options.code:
r = eng.gfx.Renderer.new(1280, 720)   # Renderer(int, int)
r.draw(mesh)                           # draw(const Mesh&)
r.draw(hud)                            # draw(const Sprite&)
options.outcome: Compiles. One Ember name per C++ name, and each call runs the declaration it compiles as a call of, taken alone (object, count, names, types after coercions, call words), choosing as an interface's instances are chosen. A call that fits none, or two equally, is E2070 naming each C++ declaration.

options.code:
r = eng.gfx.Renderer.new_int_int(1280, 720)
r.draw_Mesh(mesh)
r.draw_Sprite(hud)
options.outcome: Compiles. Each overload is its own Ember function, named from C++ types the program never wrote, and the names change when the header renames a type.

options.code:
unsafe overlay cpp "renderer.hpp":
    class Renderer:
        rename new(width, height) as sized
        rename draw(mesh) as draw_mesh
        rename draw(sprite) as draw_sprite
options.outcome: Without the overlay every overload is skipped, and `r.draw(mesh)` is a 'skipped: overloaded' diagnostic. With it, `r.draw_mesh(mesh)` compiles; today's `rename` grammar takes a name only, so the grammar would have to change too.

decisions.parameters_in_order: 1. The three goals: A keeps C++'s names and costs nothing while running, with no word added; B and C add names the program must write or keep. 2. Safety: A refuses a call no declaration fits or two fit equally and never guesses; all three are safe. 3. Compile time first: A is decided when compiling, a direct call of the chosen thunk. 4. A written word only for meaning: B's type-built names and C's renames are bookkeeping, not meaning. 5. The ordinary program: A is the C++ program's own lines; B is longer and breaks when a type is renamed; C needs an overlay line per overload before anything works. 6. Consistency: FFI-39b already selects `super.init`'s constructor by arity and argument types; TYP-24 already chooses among one name's interface instances by the call's arguments; FFI-48 refuses only the overloads a call cannot tell apart; FFI-44 imports classes automatically; FFI-40 and FFI-41 keep C++'s names.
decisions.recommendation: A, written as FFI-39b's selection extended to every call of an overloaded C++ name, with TYP-26 stating why a header's overloads are not the program's (principle 6).

owner_short.one_line: A C++ class with two constructors and two `draw(...)` overloads: what Ember calls them, and which one `r.draw(mesh)` runs.
owner_short.step_table:
| step | who | what happens | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | importer | reads `Renderer()`, `Renderer(int, int)`, `draw(const Mesh&)`, `draw(const Sprite&)` | one `new` and one `draw` on `Renderer` |
| 2 | program | writes `Renderer.new(1280, 720)` and `r.draw(mesh)` | no new word |
| 3 | compiler | keeps the overloads the call would compile against, one at a time (count, names, types, `ref mut` / `owns`) | `Renderer(int, int)`, `draw(const Mesh&)` |
| 4 | compiler | if several are left, takes the one whose types are the arguments' own; if none, or still two, an error | an error names each C++ declaration |
| 5 | program runs | a direct call of that overload | the same cost as the C++ call |
owner_short.today: Nothing says. Read literally, two functions of one name are an error, and only `super.init` picks a C++ constructor by its arguments.
options: A: one name per C++ name; the call picks by what it writes, as C++ does and as `super.init` already does
B: one name per overload, built from its types (`draw_Mesh`, `new_int_int`)
C: overloads skipped unless an overlay renames each one
owner_short.recommendation: A: the C++ program's own calls work unchanged, nothing runs while the program runs, and an unclear call is refused with the candidates named.

decisions.title: How an overlay entry names one of several C++ declarations alike in name, parameter count and parameter names
decisions.problem: An overlay entry is matched by name, parameter count and parameter names (FFI-12), and contract words take the place of types (GRM-35). That tells apart overloads that differ in count or names, but not `set(const char* name, float value)` from `set(const char* name, int value)`, nor `push(const T& value)` from `push(T&& value)`. Which declaration an entry vouches for is meaning the compiler cannot guess, so only a written word or a refusal remain.

options.outcome: Compiles. One line makes both overloads safe to call, including one its writer may never have looked at, and both must take the same contract words.

Compiles. Each line writes the parameters as the import maps them, so it names one declaration and is checked against it. The untyped line fits both and is E5010, naming both; entries whose names already differ are written as today.
Refused, and no line can name either overload. Both stay unsafe to call, with no place to write their `@safety`.
Compiles. Each overload is named by C++ text in a string: a second spelling, in another language, of what a parameter list already says.

decisions.parameters_in_order: 1. The three goals: b keeps the overlay readable as Ember and costs nothing while running. 2. Safety: a lets one line vouch for an overload its writer never named (verdict 131's problem); b, c and d refuse an entry that names no single declaration. 3. Compile time first: all four are decided when compiling. 4. A written word only for meaning: which declaration a line vouches for is meaning. b writes it only where the names do not already tell; c leaves it impossible to write, an exemption because syntax is missing (ODR 13's lesson). 5. The ordinary overlay: unchanged under b; d adds an attribute line per overload. 6. Consistency: b is Ember's own spelling of a parameter (`value: f32`, `ref mut v: Vec3`), and overlays already write types in `@ffi(macro_fn)` entries (checklist 11); d is a second spelling.
decisions.recommendation: b: an entry describes one declaration, and writes its parameters and result as the import maps them only where name, count and parameter names fit several; one that still fits several is E5010 naming them.

owner_short.one_line: Two C++ overloads with the same parameter names, `set(const char* name, float value)` and `set(const char* name, int value)`: how an overlay line says which one it vouches for.
owner_short.step_table:
| step | who | what happens | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | overlay writer | writes `fn set(name: borrowed nul_terminated, value)` | it fits both overloads |
| 2 | compiler | refuses it, naming both C++ declarations | error |
| 3 | overlay writer | writes `fn set(name: *c_char borrowed nul_terminated, value: f32)`, and the same line with `value: c_int` | each line names one overload |
| 4 | compiler | checks each line against its own overload, as for any entry | both overloads safe to call |
owner_short.today: Overlay lines are matched by name, count and parameter names only, so such a pair cannot be told apart, and a second line for one name is an error.
options: a: one line covers every overload it fits
b: the line writes the parameters' Ember types, as Ember writes a function's first line
c: refuse, with no way to vouch for either overload
d: write the C++ signature in an attribute, `@ffi(cpp="set(const char*, float)")`
owner_short.recommendation: b: Ember's own spelling of a parameter, written only where the names do not already tell the overloads apart.

Check with `ember bind --emit-cpp` and a run printing which overload ran.

`L3015` for an overloaded C++ name is given once per declaration, naming every other call. Its message gives an entry line that compiles: with types where the names do not tell the overloads apart.

`ember.overlays` records a fingerprint for each declaration of an overloaded name, whose key format is the lead's tooling; a change to one overload in the header is `E5010` only for that overload's entry.

Whether `c_int`, `c_long` and the other target-sized C types are distinct Ember types or aliases. If aliases, `f(int)` / `f(long)` on MSVC import with one Ember signature: every call is `E2070` and no entry can name one.
`E2070`'s code and message for an imported overload set (the code table says 'ambiguous interface method'): the lead's wording, naming each C++ declaration.
out.notes:
Outcome reasoning: the call selection is decided by existing properties, not a new choice. FFI-39b already selects a C++ constructor by arity and argument types. TYP-24 (p04-types.md 560-566) already chooses among one name's interface instances by a call's arguments, exact types before coercions, with ties `E2070`. FFI-48's row (p21-annex-c.md 90) refuses only the overloads a call cannot tell apart, which presumes the others import. FFI-44 imports classes automatically, and FFI-40 and FFI-41 keep C++ names. So options B and C contradict the spec as written. FFI-12 (p16-ffi.md 322-323) already tells the question's own overlay entries apart by count and parameter names; the finder missed that, and FFI-30c's 'second entry for one name' was the real block there. One part needed a choice: how an entry names an overload alike in name, count and parameter names. Hence decided_by_parameters, with both choices recorded in decisions for the owner's later review. Nothing goes into the specification before that review.

Left alone because they are outside the allowed rules, and not holes caused by these edits:
(1) FFI-30c's words still say 'for one name'. GRM-35's new sentence makes `override` and the second-entry rule count by declaration; the lead may align FFI-30c's wording in the hardening.
(2) FFI-48's row says 'rename one in the overlay', but `rename` and `hide` take a name only, so they act on every declaration of the name and cannot rename one overload. This is a pre-existing gap. A wrapper in an overlay `extend` block (FFI-13) gives one overload a name of its own through the new selection.
(3) FFI-55's record keys show one name per declaration.
(4) The const/non-const pair called through a changeable name is `E2070` under these words. It is K47's question (J8-05), which the group says to ask after this one; through a read-only name the const one is chosen.
(5) Not stated anywhere: how C++ copy and move constructors import (a `Texture.new(other)` pair), and whether C++ default arguments import. Both are separate gaps; if default arguments import, a tie between `f(a)` and `f(a, b = 0)` is `E2070`, as C++ also calls it ambiguous.
(6) Whether verdict 159 (a constructor's argument takes no word) reaches C++ constructors is not decided here. The selection counts whatever words the call rule requires.

Nothing was run, and every claim that would need a run is in to_verify. Per the rules, characters were not counted.

holes.today: Undecided, and refused if read literally (TYP-26 p04-types.md 867-868, E1030).
holes.with_edit: FFI-39b's added sentence chooses among 'the declarations it would compile as a call of'. Outside `unsafe:`, push(int16_t) has no entry, so a call of it does not compile there (FFI-2 p16-ffi.md 33-41, E5002). push(int32_t) compiles, since i16 reaches i32 by widening (TYP-5 rule 1, p04-types.md 74). Read plainly, the first call runs push(int32_t) and the identical call inside `unsafe:` runs push(int16_t), the exact fit. The parenthetical ('its object, and its arguments' number, names, types after coercions and words') can instead be read as the whole test: that picks push(int16_t) both times and refuses the first line with E5002. The words do not say which reading holds.
holes.what_goes_wrong: Under the plain reading, one call runs a different C++ function depending on whether it sits in `unsafe:`. FFI-11c (p16-ffi.md 318-321) makes a header safe one function at a time; moving a call out of `unsafe:` once one overload is vouched silently changes what runs (here 12000 >> 8 = 46 is stored), with no diagnostic. The same mechanism applies to every check around a call. In a `@noalloc` function, a declaration with no `effects=[]` is E4001 (p10-effects.md 175), so an overload declared `@ffi(effects=[])` and reached by widening runs there, while the exact one runs elsewhere. The thread and view rules work the same way. C++ chooses by the call alone and the object's constness, never by what surrounds the call.

holes.fix_hint: Which declaration a call runs depends only on the call: its object's permission, and its arguments' number, names, types and words. Unsafe code, effects, threads and views are checked on the chosen declaration afterwards.

outs.notes:
I read the edit's three sentences against every program in the answer and its four siblings: all stated outcomes hold, with the caveats listed in checked. Nothing was run.

The high hole: TYP-26's added sentence imports a C++ overload set as one name, but only calls are decided. An Ember class that overrides one virtual of an overloaded set (FFI-39) then falls under CLS-4's by-name rule ('a method named like an inherited one replaces it'), which reads as replacing every declaration of that name. That is undecided, and if the trampoline does it, it is type confusion inside safe code.

The medium holes:
- Hole 2: the plain reading of 'the declarations it would compile as a call of' lets the checks around a call choose the overload (unsafe code, `@noalloc`, threads, views). Moving a call out of `unsafe:`, as FFI-11c's adoption path does, then silently changes which C++ function runs.
- Hole 3: the const/non-const accessor pair through a changeable name is E2070 with no spelling that reaches the non-const declaration.
- Hole 4: an integer literal against int/float overloads is E2070, where C++ runs the int one.

Holes 3 and 4 are refusals, not unsafety. They are medium because they refuse ordinary C++ calls and contradict the answer's stated intent.

Lows: FFI-30c's wording clashes with GRM-35's new counting; an overloaded name used as a function value is undecided; a member defined outside its class reads literally as two declarations; a use after hand-over at an overloaded call gets E2070 instead of E3040.

Pre-existing items I saw, which are not holes of this edit:
- FFI-40's 'where the type is movable' for a class with a user destructor and no move constructor.
- `rename`/`hide` act on every declaration of a name.
- FFI-55's record keys.
- Clang's `__attribute__((overloadable))` in C headers is outside the edit, which covers C++ only.

The JSON sibling's `w.value(7)` depends on whether int64_t maps to i64 or c_long; the answer already lists this in to_verify, and C++ is ambiguous there too.

checked: J8-04 without the overlay. Confirmed: it compiles under the edit. `Renderer.new(1280, 720)`: `Renderer(int, int)` is the only two-argument constructor (the literals take `c_int`, LEX-16 p02-lexical.md 139-141). `r.draw(mesh)` and `r.draw(hud)`: `const T&` imports as a plain parameter (FFI-40 p21-annex-c.md 161-163), so each argument fits one `draw`. The calls stay unsafe with no entry (FFI-2 p16-ffi.md 40-41), and L3015 follows verdicts 125 and 134.

J8-04 with the overlay. Confirmed through FFI-12 (p16-ffi.md 322-323), which matches on name, count and parameter names, together with GRM-35's added sentence. But FFI-30c's words (p16-ffi.md 221-222) still say 'any other second entry for one name is E5010' (hole 5).

JSON writer sibling. Confirmed on MSVC: `int64_t` is `long long`, which maps to `i64` (FFI-8 p16-ffi.md 173). TYP-24 p04-types.md 563-566 picks exact types first. TYP-5 rule 1 gives `i32` to `i64`. There is no int-to-float coercion, and nothing converts to `bool` (p04-types.md 74-102). On LP64 Linux, `int64_t` is `long`, which maps to `c_long`, and FFI-8 does not say whether `c_long` is `i64`. If it is a distinct type, `w.value(7)` ties. This gap was already there before the edit, and the edit lists it in to_verify.

Asset cache sibling. Confirmed: `T&&` imports as `owns x: T` (FFI-40). E3028 refuses a missing or extra word (p17a-codes.md 138; verdicts 146 and 147), so the word at the call picks one `add`, and a later use of `splash` is E3040.
Shader sibling. Confirmed for `s.set(c"tint", 0.5)` and `s.set(c"mode", mode)`, and the untyped entry is E5010. The same header called with a literal, `s.set(c"mode", 2)`, is E2070 (hole 1).

Config sibling. Confirmed through a read-only parameter (IV.11 step 3, p04-types.md 860-863; FFI-40a p21-annex-c.md 164-171). Through a name that may change the config the call is E2070 (pre-existing hole, K47).
Readability claim. It holds for the question's program. It fails for literal arguments to `int`/`float` overload pairs (hole 1).
Cost claim. Confirmed: the choice is made when compiling, and each call is one direct thunk call (FFI-3, FFI-17, BLD-FFI-4). There is no table and nothing runs.

Verdicts the edit claims to keep. 125, 131, 146 and 147 are kept. 132 is kept per declaration, except for a const/non-const pair with identical parameters and result, which no entry can name (hole 7). Whether 159 reaches `new` is left open, as the edit says.

My own programs: `store(int16_t)`/`store(int64_t)` called with `i8`; namespace `dot(Vec2)`/`dot(Vec3)`; `fill(Circle)`/`fill(Square)` given a `Shape`; `put(Mesh)`/`put(const Mesh&)`; a top-level entry for a member; vouching per declaration; an `extend` method `draw` beside the header's; `super.init` by arity; `int`/`float` pairs called with literals (a shader and `super.init`); a safe and an unsafe overload around `unsafe:`; an overloaded name as a function value; overriding one overload of a C++ virtual; overriding both; a header adding an overload with the same parameter name; a const/non-const `visit` pair; a typed entry for a name declared once; a function redeclared in one header; `int`/`long`/`long long` on MSVC.

The last two programs found nothing new. First, `set(Falloff)` / `set(int)`: there is no integer-to-enum coercion, so each argument fits one declaration. Second, `Button::move(Point)` hiding `Widget::move`: IV.11 step 2 takes the inherent method before the base's, as C++ hiding does.

matrix.how_kept: TYP-26's added sentence (p04-types.md after line 868) lets a header's declarations of one name import as that name. FFI-39b's added sentence (p21-annex-c.md after line 130) chooses among them by each declaration's fit taken alone, then by TYP-24's exact-before-coercion rule (p04-types.md 563-566). No construct is named. The property stops short for literal arguments (hole 1), uses that are not calls (hole 3) and overrides (hole 4).

matrix.guarantee: As fast as C: the choice is made when compiling; per call, one direct call of the chosen overload's thunk

There is no table and no check while running. Compile time adds one fit test per candidate declaration at each call (to measure). An argument whose kind is only known while running fits no overload, so nothing is ever chosen at run time.

matrix.guarantee: Readable and easy: the ordinary program is no longer and no harder than today

Nothing is added at a call. A written type is asked for only where an overlay entry must say which declaration it vouches for, which is meaning.
